## #1624/#1625: Gitea listings that move and budgets on incremental runs (Opus implementer, 2026-10-22)

- **What "the watermark is the oldest examined record" (spec #1618 ruling A6) stores.** *Ruling:*
  the oldest record examined is where the next run continues (`below`, in an optional catch-up
  beside the watermark); the watermark itself (`pulls_updated_to`, `commits_since`) stays where it
  was, and the catch-up also keeps the newest record examined (`newest`). The next run reads only
  the window from `below` down to the watermark, under the same budget, and adopts `newest` as the
  watermark once it reaches it. *Reasoning:* both walks read newest first, so the records a budget
  leaves unread are the older ones, between the old watermark and the oldest examined. A watermark
  moved to the oldest examined would have the next walk stop exactly where they begin; one left
  alone with nothing else would have each run spend its budget on the same newest 200 again; and
  `CONTEXT.md` defines a watermark as a position that only advances as work completes, which a
  watermark moved back to the oldest examined is not. A6's wording is #1715. The catch-up fields are
  optional, so the cursor stays version 3. *Reversing:* medium, the two walks and the two cursor
  structs; a cursor holding a catch-up would then lose its window once.
- **Where a pull-request catch-up starts.** *Ruling:* on the page the budget stopped on, trusted
  only when that page's first record is newer than the resume point; otherwise from page 1.
  *Reasoning:* from page 1 the window is reached only after skipping every record the cut-short walk
  read, which at a budget of 1,000, or 200 on a Gitea capped at 10 a page, spends the whole page cap
  on skips and the catch-up never progresses. An edit shifts records down and only repeats a row; a
  deletion or a larger page shifts unread records above the hint, which the first-record check
  catches. *Reversing:* low, `walk_pulls`'s start.
- **What a run holding a catch-up reads above it.** *Ruling:* nothing until the window closes; the
  run that closes it walks on from `newest` with what is left of the budget. *Reasoning:* one window
  at a time keeps the cursor to one gap. Two gaps would need a list of windows. *Reversing:* low.
- **Commits.** *Ruling:* the catch-up names the branches not finished in walk order. The cut one is
  read from `below` (the `until=` bound, server-side and inclusive, now live-asserted) down to the
  watermark, the rest from their heads. Branches that move while a catch-up is pending are walked from
  `newest`, not from the newest commit the catch-up just read on another branch. *Reasoning:* the head
  the cursor stores has already moved, so without the list nothing walks the cut branch again;
  without `until=` the catch-up re-lists every commit already delivered and has the cap problem
  above. *Reversing:* medium, as the first ruling.
- **A page cap on an incremental walk.** *Ruling:* it cuts the walk short like the budget and leaves
  a catch-up. A full sync still stops quietly (ADR-0003). *Reasoning:* the cap otherwise loses
  updates the same way the budget did once more than 1,000 records changed. *Reversing:* low.
- **Repository listing key.** *Ruling:* `sort=id&order=asc`. *Reasoning:* A1 asks for `created`,
  or `id` where the pinned Gitea offers it. 1.27.3's `repoSearch` offers `id`, and ids are unique
  where two repositories can share a `created` second. *Reversing:* low, one query parameter.
- **A re-read of an unlisted branch that fails with anything but 404.** *Ruling:* the failure takes
  the path any failed read in the repository walk takes (`RepoError::from`). *Reasoning:* the branch
  has not been shown to be gone, and keeping its stored head without reading it would hide a
  server fault behind a run reported `Ok`. *Reversing:* low.
- **The docker-free fake's single-branch read.** *Ruling:* a branch the state does not hold answers
  404, as Gitea does (measured for #724), not the catch-all empty page. *Reasoning:* `[]` read as
  "still there" once the walk began re-reading unlisted branches. *Reversing:* n/a.

### #1624/#1625 review rulings (merge-manager, Opus, 2026-10-22)

- **#1624's "the watermark after the first run is the oldest examined record".** *Fork:* hold the
  PR until the code moves `pulls_updated_to` / `commits_since` to the oldest record examined, or
  accept the catch-up's `below` as meeting it. *Ruling:* met in intent, ticked with this note. The
  criterion contradicts the same ticket's other clause, "all 260 mirrored after two runs, the 40
  reading merged": both walks read newest first and stop below the watermark, so a watermark set
  to the oldest examined (record 61 of 260) makes the second run read 61 to 260 again and never
  the 60 under it. The code cannot satisfy both, and A6's own reasoning ("the next run must
  continue, not skip ... the delta complete over several runs") is the clause the catch-up meets.
  The oldest examined record is stored as the resume point (`*_catching_up.below`) and the tests
  assert it after the first run; the watermark field keeps its meaning, everything at or before it
  delivered. A6's wording is #1715, relabelled `ready-for-agent` because the spec ruling is wrong
  as worded (brief: a wrong spec gets a follow-up). *Reversing:* medium, as the implementer's
  first ruling above.
- **"The cursor version stays `3`".** *Ruling:* honestly met. `GiteaCursor::parse` takes any
  `"v":3` envelope and none of the cursor structs denies unknown fields. A version-3 cursor from
  before #1624 reads with both catch-ups `None` (serde default), which is today's incremental run;
  a cursor written by this code and read by an older build parses too, the catch-up ignored, and
  its watermark is still the conservative one (nothing above it is claimed delivered), so the older
  build only repeats its own budget bug and loses nothing it would not have lost anyway. A
  catch-up-free cursor serialises byte-identical to before (`catching_up` absent,
  `cursor::tests::empty_fields_are_omitted` asserts it). *Reversing:* n/a.
- **§10.8.** *Ruling:* no entry owed. `crates/knobas-source-gitea/**` and its cursor are not on
  §10.8's frozen list (the cursor is an opaque adapter string, §4.2), and nothing in
  `knobas-source`, `knobas-http`, a migration or the IPC changed. The §4.2 Gitea row now says
  "Amended by #1624" for the catch-ups, the repository order and `until=`, as #764 and #1138 did
  for theirs. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **Live re-run after the rebase.** *Ruling:* required, `just gitea-live` and
  `just gitea-live-capped` re-run on the rebased head. The rebase brought #1709's (issue #1647)
  `images.env` rename into `seed-gitea.sh`, `live-lib.sh` and the justfile's `gitea-live-capped`
  compose calls, and #1712's (issue #1622) new `knobas-source` module; both suites use the first
  and link the second (working model, *A PR at the real systems' edge carries its live run*).
  *Reversing:* n/a.
- **A pull-request page hint whose first record sits on `below`'s own second.** *Ruling:* left as
  is: the walk restarts from page 1, which costs at most one run that reads no new records when
  more than the page cap lies above the window, and then makes progress from the cap's last page.
  Trusting `first == below` would be unsafe, because an unread record on that second can sit on an
  earlier page. *Reversing:* low.

## #1665/#1668: the launcher box as a combobox, and the Session lifecycle fixes (Opus implementer, 2026-10-22)

- **The value suggestions list.** *Fork:* the ticket names the results and the chain as the lists
  the box controls; the suggestion list under the box is a third one the arrows walk. *Ruling:*
  included. While suggestions are open the arrows and `Enter` drive them (`suggestionKey` runs
  first in `onkeydown`), so a box that still named a results row would announce a row `Enter`
  does not open. The box controls the list in `onkeydown`'s order: suggestions, then the chain,
  then the results. *Reversing:* low, one branch in `controlled`.

  is, so the popup is never collapsed; an expanded flag that tracked "has an active option"
  would say the list was gone while it is on screen saying *Searching…*. *Reversing:* low.
- **`aria-autocomplete="list"`.** *Ruling:* added beside the attributes the ticket names: the
  lists are filtered by what is typed and the box's text is never completed inline, which is
  what `list` says. *Reversing:* low.
- **`tabindex="-1"` on the results and chain lists.** *Ruling:* kept; the ticket asks only that
  the lists keep `role="listbox"`, and dropping it would change what a click on a list's padding
  does. *Reversing:* low.
- **What the residue test enrols.** *Fork:* add LinkDialog to the table by hand, or widen the
  rule. *Ruling:* widened: a component is enrolled when it has a `$effect` **or** constructs a

  enrols LinkDialog, TfLinkTo and TfBlockDialog, each with an `exercise` that types.

  `tf/job/TfLinkTo.svelte`, which the ticket does not name. *Ruling:* fixed here, the same

- **The `launcher-hotkey` witness driver.** *Fork:* the driver asserts the focused box's role is

## #1666 (PR #1718): shell database state written only on change

- **Is the `App.test.svelte.ts` re-send a test fix or an ordering bug?** (merge-manager on
  Sonnet). *Ruling:* a test fix. `inbox.start()` subscribes before `lifecycle.start()` arms the
  database, and the inbox is seeded by `refresh()` at the first `ready`, which reads whatever
  arrived earlier. An `activity:new` that beats the listener is only possible before `ready`,
  and the seed then reads it. The old test sent its signal after `ready` with the fake database
  already up, which raced the listener's registration; the second reseed hid that. *Reversing:*
  none, test-only.
- **`retry()` writes `starting` only if the state is still `failed`** (the ticket's second
  alternative). *Ruling:* kept. A failed-to-failed retry still shows Starting (nothing moved the
  state, so the write happens), and the poll repairs it as before. A pre-await write was
  rejected: it would flash Starting before the backend accepts the retry. *Reversing:* low.
- **The surviving mutant (event handler assigning `state.db` directly).** *Ruling:* owed and
  cheap: added `the same ready event twice seeds once`; the mutant now dies. *Reversing:* none.

## #1623: the Jira walk orders by `created` and fails on a shrinking total (Opus implementer, 2026-10-22)

- **What the shrink is measured against.** The ticket says "the total at the end of the walk is
  below the total at its start". *Ruling:* every answer is compared with the largest `total` the
  walk has seen, and the first one below it fails the run then. It catches every case the ticket's
  rule catches, plus an issue filed and another deleted mid-walk, which leave the end total equal
  to the start with the hole still there. Failing at the first such answer saves the rest of the
  walk's requests. *Reversing:* low, one comparison in `refuse_a_shrunk_total`.
- **Where the check sits.** `PageWalk` ends on an empty page without handing it out, and
  `crates/knobas-http/**` is frozen. *Ruling:* the check sits inside the adapter's fetch closure,
  so it reads the empty last page's total too; `knobas-http` is untouched. *Reversing:* low.
- **A deletion behind the cursor, which skips nothing, fails the run too.** *Ruling:* accepted.
  `total` cannot tell the two apart, and A5 already weighs it: a failed run costs one re-fetch, a
  false `Ok` costs a tombstoned live ticket. *Reversing:* none needed.
- **Incremental runs.** *Ruling:* the refusal is unconditional, as the page cap's is. A stepped-over
  issue on an incremental run sits below the advanced watermark and is lost for good, so the
  incremental case is worse than the full one, not safer. *Reversing:* low.
- **A tiebreak after `created`.** *Superseded by #1720 below: an edit reorders a tie, measured.*
  *Ruling:* none. The ticket pins the literal `ORDER BY created
  ASC`, `created` has millisecond resolution, and a second key would also need mockd's grammar to
  grow. *Reversing:* low, one clause.
- **mockd.** Its JQL subset accepted only `ORDER BY updated`, so every adapter test against it
  would have been a 400. *Ruling:* the subset gains `ORDER BY created ASC|DESC`, sorted on
  `created`, recorded in `docs/contract.md`'s "Amendments from the Jira walk order" with pointers
  at §4.2, the #345 amendment's row and §5. *Reversing:* low.
- **Where the engine's sweep gate is asserted.** `knobas-sync` has no dependency on the Jira crate.
  *Ruling:* `sweep.rs`'s own fake gains a `fails` switch, and the test asserts that a full sync
  failing after it emitted tombstones nothing. The adapter's own tests assert that the shrink
  fails the run, and `Source::sync`'s `Err` is the wire between the two. *Reversing:* low.
- **What the live run witnesses.** Nothing lets a test edit an issue between two of the adapter's
  own page requests. *Ruling:* two raw-`/search` tests on the seeded Jira check what the fake
  claims about Jira: a label edit moves an issue to the end of `ORDER BY updated ASC` and nowhere
  in `ORDER BY created ASC`, and after a filed sub-task is deleted, a page past the new end
  answers 200 with no issues and the smaller total. *Reversing:* low.

## #1623: merge review of #1719 (Opus merge-manager, 2026-10-22)

### Failing an incremental run on a shrunk total, confirmed

**The fork:** the refusal applies to incremental runs too, so any deletion (or exit from a `jql_filter`) between two of a run's `/search` requests fails that run. Can a busy Jira fail every run?

**Ruling:** confirmed. The next run recovers: a failed run commits neither cursor nor items, so the next one repeats the same `since`, and a deletion happens once. Only a shrink between two requests of the same run fails it. An incremental run that fits on one page (`page_size` 100 by default) makes one `/search` request, because `Offset` stops when the rows read reach `total`, so a shrink can't happen inside it. Every run fails only when a shrink falls inside each multi-page walk. That fits a full sync of a large instance under a `jql_filter` on a field that changes often. Spec #1618 ruling A5 weighed that case and rejected an in-run re-walk, and the run's `Protocol` error is `SyncOutcome::Error`, which the next tick retries. Letting incremental runs through would lose the stepped-over issue for good: it sits below the advanced watermark.

**Cost of reversing:** low, one condition on the refusal.

### The contract amendment belongs in the contract body, not §10.8

**The fork:** a §10.8 entry is one file under `docs/contract/10.8/`, or a body amendment with #112 pointers.

**Ruling:** the body. The diff touches no surface §10.8 freezes: no `crates/knobas-source/src/**`, `crates/knobas-http/**`, migration, IPC schema, or `knobas-app` `error.rs`/`profile.rs`. The change supersedes the §4.2 Jira cursor row, the #345 amendment's JQL line, and §5's mockd JQL subset. Under #112's convention the old text stays and gets an italic pointer, which the #345 amendment already did to the same row. The rebase's hand-resolved conflict keeps main's #1624 text in the Gitea cell and the #1623 pointer in the Jira cell. No conflict markers remain.

**Cost of reversing:** none.

### No `just jira-live` re-run after the rebase, confirmed

**The fork:** the live run is from `0ee671f3` (base `c949263a`). The branch was then rebased onto `cf2b4193`.

**Ruling:** no re-run. `c949263a..cf2b4193` is #1714 (Gitea), #1717 (frontend) and #1666 (frontend), plus `CONTEXT.md`, `testenv/README.md` and a desktop-witness driver. None of these is something `jira-live` exercises (working model, amended 2026-10-12). #1709's `images.env`/`live-lib.sh` change (`6240852d`) is already in `c949263a`, so the run used it.

**Cost of reversing:** one `just jira-live`.

### Ties on `created` stay open, filed as #1720

**The fork:** among issues that share a `created` stamp, Jira's order is its index's tiebreak, and an edit may change it.

**Ruling:** the implementer's no-tiebreak ruling stands, because the ticket pins the literal `ORDER BY created ASC`. The open question is filed as #1720 (`backlog`): check on the seeded Jira, then add a unique tiebreak if one is needed.

**Cost of reversing:** low.

## #1627: a Kuma write whose acknowledgement was lost (Opus implementer, 2026-10-22)

- **Which failures after the emit become `Unconfirmed`.** The ticket says "any transport failure".
  *Ruling:* every class the ack poll can fail with: `Unreachable`, `Protocol` with any status or
  none, `Unauthorized`, and an `Unconfirmed` from a pong. The poll's status is kept
  (`once_emitted`). A `400 Session ID unknown` on the poll means the session went *after* the
  packet was taken, and a `401` from a proxy in front of Kuma says nothing about the packet. Left
  as they were, the first is recorded as refused and the second waits for a credential and then
  sends the create again. *Reversing:* low, one match.
- **When the emit "went out", for the deadline.** *Ruling:* from the moment its POST starts, not
  from when the POST returns `Ok`. A deadline that drops the POST in flight may drop a packet Kuma
  already took, which is `knobas_http::classify::once_sent`'s reading of a timeout after connect.
  The flag is cleared again by the two refusals that prove Kuma did nothing (`400` to the emit's
  own POST, *You are not logged in.*), so a deadline on the fresh login that follows keeps the
  status-less `Protocol` it had before. *Reversing:* low, one line moves.
- **An ack that arrived but cannot be read** (`answer()`'s parse failure). *Ruling:* left as
  status-less `Protocol` here. The ack arrived, so this is not a lost acknowledgement, and the
  pinned Kuma never produces one. It is the one Kuma path left that can record a write that may
  have landed as refused, and #1721 (backlog) holds the fork. *Reversing:* low.
- **Pause and resume after a post-emit deadline.** Before this change they were refused; now they
  are `Unconfirmed`, which their `resend_harmless` delivery turns into an `unreachable` wait, sent
  again on a later tick. The socket's old doc argued against exactly that wait (a minute of every
  tick against a drifted Kuma). *Ruling:* accepted. The ticket asks for it, a pause that landed
  must not read as refused, and #1628's ladder is what bounds how often it goes again.
  *Reversing:* low.
- **The `SourceError::Unconfirmed` doc comment in the frozen crate.** It said the variant is
  "raised only by `knobas_http`". *Ruling:* rewritten and booked in
  `docs/contract/10.8/1627-kuma-lost-ack-unconfirmed.md`, because it changes what the clause
  commits to (who may raise the variant), which #518's rule sends to the gate as code.
  *Reversing:* low, one comment.
- **What `just kuma-live` witnesses.** ADR-0013 counts a dropped connection among what a live
  instance can be made to do, so a fake Kuma alone would not do for the ticket's case. *Ruling:*
  `live_kuma.rs` puts a relay between the adapter and the real container that drops every request
  after the `add` has been answered (`LosingLink`). The real Kuma creates the monitor, the write
  answers `Unconfirmed` (`Unreachable` with the parent's `socket.rs`, run and recorded in the PR),
  and Kuma holds exactly one monitor by that name. `kuma_write_live.rs` also asserts one attached
  monitor for the happy-path create. The reaped-before-ack, never-acknowledged and on-the-wire
  deadline cases need Kuma itself to reap or stall between two packets, and stay with
  `socket::session_tests`' fake. *Reversing:* low, one test and its relay.
- **Kuma's login limit in `just kuma-live`.** With the lost-ack test added, one run's second
  binary had its `kuma-monitor.sh add` refused with *Too frequently, try again later.*: the suite
  sits near Kuma's twenty logins a minute, and the new test spends logins of its own. *Ruling:*
  the lost-ack test skips the pre-delete the create test makes (the seed the recipe runs first
  sweeps the name), and `testenv/kuma-monitor.mjs` waits 61 s and logs in once more when its
  login is refused for the limit, rather than failing a test on the fixture's budget. The re-run
  that followed did not need the wait. Re-adding #864's 61 s sleep between the binaries would
  have cost every run a minute. *Reversing:* low, one branch in the helper.
- **Merge-manager review (Opus, 2026-10-22): pause and resume sent again after a post-emit
  deadline.** *Ruling:* right under ADR-0012 as amended by #1125. Kuma's `pauseMonitor` and
  `resumeMonitor` set the monitor's `active` flag and stop or restart its check, so a second
  arrival leaves the state the first set; `WriteOp::delivery` already says `resend_harmless: true`
  for both ("the same state twice is one"). `store::due` takes a source's head write, so a later
  opposite op stays behind the waiting one. The cost is time, not state: a Kuma that takes the
  emit and never acknowledges it spends up to `CALL_BUDGET` (60 s) of the sequential `flush_all`
  per attempt until #1628's ladder spaces the attempts (noted on #1628). *Reversing:* low.
- **Merge-manager review: the login-limit retry in `testenv/kuma-monitor.mjs`.** *Ruling:* sound.
  It matches only Kuma's own refusal text inside the login callback, waits once, and a second
  refusal still fails the helper with Kuma's words; the wait is logged. It cannot hide an adapter
  that spends too many logins: the adapter's budget is witnessed by
  `more_writes_in_a_minute_than_kuma_allows_logins_all_land`, which drives the adapter directly,
  not the helper. It also covers the cause #1727 reports (`Scratch::drop`'s delete refused for the
  limit), since the delete goes through the same login. *Reversing:* low.
## #1630: one rate limiter per instance, and a limiter wait reported as the local quota (Opus implementer, 2026-10-22)

- **Reserved for Björn, ruled by implementer on Opus: the frozen-surface change to
  `crates/knobas-http/**`** (waived by Björn 2026-10-22, review handoff). *Ruling:* one new
  module, `limiter.rs`, with an additive public `InstanceLimiter` and `LocalQuota`, plus a
  `test-util` `HttpClient::with_send_budget`; booked in
  `docs/contract/10.8/1630-knobas-http-one-limiter-per-instance.md`. No `HttpConfig` field or
  adapter changes. *Reversing:* low; the limiter goes back into the client.
- **"Governor's keyed form".** Governor's `RateLimiter::keyed` holds one quota for every key, so
  it cannot give a Jira origin 5/s and a Gitea origin 10/s, or let the stricter of two
  configurations govern one origin. Both are requirements of the spec. *Ruling:* a process-wide
  map keyed by `url::Origin`, holding one governor direct limiter per origin. That is still a
  keyed limiter in `knobas-http`, which is A3's actual fork (as against a cached `Source`). The
  spec's requirement wins over its parenthesis. *Reversing:* low, inside one module.
- **What "stricter" means when the two quotas cross** (one has the higher rate, the other the
  higher burst). *Ruling:* field by field: the lower rate and the lower burst. A server that
  tolerates one configuration's burst says nothing about the other's. *Reversing:* low, one
  function.
- **Whether a quota can loosen again.** *Ruling:* no, not for the life of the process. A source
  edited to a looser quota gets it from the next start. The quota has to outlive the clients that
  use it: if the entry died with its last client, the next client built a moment later would get
  a fresh burst, which is SPI-2 again. Nothing identifies a configuration to the http crate, so it
  cannot retire a stale one. *Reversing:* moderate; it needs a configuration identity passed in.
- **What a tightening does to the limiter it replaces.** Governor cannot change the quota of a
  limiter it has already built. *Ruling:* a new limiter at the merged quota, which every holder
  waits on from its next request. It starts with its own (stricter) burst, so a tightening hands
  out at most one stricter burst, and there are only a few tightenings in a process's life.
  Draining the new limiter was rejected: it buys nothing in practice and makes the first request
  after a tightening wait. *Reversing:* low, one line.
- **A limiter wait that runs the budget out before a retry.** *Ruling:* the call fails with the
  previous attempt's failure, not with the local quota, the same rule as for a retry delay that
  does not fit the budget. Only a first attempt reports `Protocol` naming the quota. The source
  has already answered by then, and if that answer was a timeout, `Unreachable` is the
  instance's own failure. *Reversing:* low, one branch.
- **How a test sees the budget run out without waiting 45 s.** *Ruling:* `with_send_budget`
  behind the existing `test-util` feature, off in every build an adapter compiles against.
  `SEND_BUDGET` stays the only budget anywhere else. *Reversing:* low.
- **Whether the change owes a live suite** (working model, "a PR at the real systems' edge").
  `knobas-http` sits under every adapter, and the shared limiter changes pacing for everything
  that builds clients for one origin. *Ruling:* yes, and `just kuma-live` is the cheapest that
  exercises it: Kuma's read half (5/s, burst 10) and its polling transport (25/s, burst 50) share
  an origin, so the run covers sharing and stricter-wins against the real product. Green.
- **Kuma's polling transport now runs at the read half's quota.** The spec's rule, but
  `KumaSocket::new`'s doc gives the reason for the higher rate. *Ruling:* the shared limiter
  follows the spec. The Kuma crate is left alone (#1627 is in flight there), and the question is
  filed as #1723 (`backlog`). *Reversing:* n/a.
- **Test servers on reused ports** (Standards review). The map never forgets an origin, so a test
  server handed a port an earlier test tightened to one a second would inherit that quota.
  *Ruling:* `CountingServer` keeps its port bound for the rest of the test process (a forgotten
  duplicate of the listener), so no later server in the binary gets it. The quota map stays
  without a test-only reset. *Reversing:* low, test code.

### #1630: merge-manager review (Opus, PR #1724, 2026-10-22)

- **A quota that only tightens until restart.** The rate fields are on every source's settings
  form, so a raised quota is silently not used until restart, and a quota tried in a draft's
  *Test connection* holds the origin down too. Before #1630 an edit applied from the next client.
  *Ruling:* merge as built, because it closes SPI-2, and file #1728 (`ready-for-agent`, since the
  form shows a value the app does not use): loosen once no live client asks for the stricter
  quota (weak registrations, no configuration identity needed), with a loosened limiter starting
  drained so that alternating sources get no fresh burst. *Reversing:* the follow-up is the
  reversal, inside `limiter.rs`.
- **#1723 (Kuma's polling transport at the read half's 5/s, burst 10).** *Ruling:* it stays
  `backlog`. The socket carries only writes, and they go through the queue, so nobody waits on
  one in the UI. A single write's dozen polls mostly fit the shared burst, `just kuma-live`'s
  `more_writes_in_a_minute_than_kuma_allows_logins_all_land` is green, and the pacing is the
  spec's stricter-wins rule. *Reversing:* relabel.
- **A local-quota failure in the write queue.** `Protocol` with no status is a refusal in
  `write_queue::retryable`, so a write the limiter held past the budget would now be refused
  instead of waiting. The spec says `Protocol`, and with serial adapters a write cannot wait that
  long today. *Ruling:* follow the spec and file #1729 (`backlog`). *Reversing:* n/a.
- **The implementer's other rulings** (origin map of direct limiters, field-by-field stricter,
  tightening without a drain, a retry keeping the previous failure, the public seam for #1631,
  `with_send_budget`, held test ports) are upheld. Lock order is `INSTANCES` then the slot's
  `paced`, and no path takes them in reverse. Nothing is awaited under either: the limiter is
  cloned out before the wait. The map holds one entry per origin. *Reversing:* n/a.

## #1670 (implementer)

### One derived map, not a `satisfies` per fixture

**The fork:** the ticket offers `satisfies` on each fixture or a handler map whose return types come from the barrel's functions.

**Ruling:** the derived map. `fake-answers.ts` holds `Answers`, one line per `invoke("<command>")` in the barrels, each `Awaited<ReturnType<typeof barrelFn>>`; `Handlers` in `fake-tauri.ts` is `{ [K in keyof Answers]?: ... } & Record<string, Handler>`. A rename in the generated mirror reaches the barrel function, then the map, then every handler. It sits outside `fake/` because that directory is globbed for feature modules. Fixture constants carry `satisfies` or an annotation only where inference widens a literal.

**Cost of reversing:** delete one file and restore `Record<string, Handler>` in 27 signatures. A command missing from `Answers` stays untyped, so a new command needs its line.

### Fields the wire sends and a fixture left out are filled with the empty value

**The fork:** typing the fixtures showed answers short of the generated type: `SourceDescriptor` (`accepts_account`, `payload_paths`, `source_actions`, `clone_from`, `url_forms`), `DiffFile.threads`, the diff block's `commentable` and `gone`, `SearchHit.state`.

**Ruling:** add them as `false`, `[]` or `null`. No reader treats the absent field differently from the empty one (`accepts_account ?? false`, `payload_paths ?? []`), so `?fake-ipc` draws what it drew. The two TeamCity `payload_paths` entries stay sparse (`kind`, `frame`) behind a cast, as `kind-registry.test.svelte.ts` does.

**Cost of reversing:** delete the added lines.

### Three casts remain where the fixture echoes the client

**The fork:** `submit_write`'s payload, `edit_asset`/`edit_route`'s property value, and `add_source`'s `auth_kind` arrive as `unknown`.

**Ruling:** cast to the generated type at the echo. The fixture sends back what the client sent; the cast says so.

**Cost of reversing:** none worth the name.

### A census test forces a line in `Answers` for every barrel command (merge-manager)

**The fork:** a command the barrels gain, with no line in `fake-answers.ts`, stays untyped and the rename guard has a hole.

**Ruling:** `fake-tauri.test.ts` compares the command names listed in `fake-answers.ts` with `barrelCommands()`, both ways. It is one test beside the existing census, which already reads the barrels; no new parser.

**Cost of reversing:** delete the test.
- **#1727: is the second half (alert_chain_live clearing leftovers) still owed?** *Fork:* delete
  `knobas-write-scratch` and the created monitor before the first run, or make the count robust.
  *Ruling:* the cause is covered by #1722's 61 s login retry, but the assertion still depended on
  other binaries' cleanup. `alert_chain_live` now counts samples only of monitors still in
  `sync.live_item`, so a monitor that was sampled by the first run and gone by the last (any
  binary's leftover) cannot move the count; every live monitor must still be sampled. A
  pre-clean would spend up to four logins of Kuma's twenty a minute and still race a sibling.
  *Reversing:* low (one query).

### #1671: merge-manager review (Sonnet, 2026-10-22)

- **The busy-save test lifts Save's `disabled` by hand.** *Ruling:* kept. Save is disabled while
  `busy`, so only a click already queued before the re-render can reach `save()` busy; that path is
  near-unreachable in the app, and the guard is harmless there. The test witnesses the store
  contract (`amend` resolves `false` when skipped, `save()` keeps the draft), not a user path.
  *Reversing:* low.
- **The #775 test now expects Flush now disabled while out.** *Ruling:* that is the ticket's intent
  (a double click sends one `flush_writes`), not a weakened assertion; the other buttons stay
  asserted enabled. The test is retitled "disables only itself". *Reversing:* low.
## #1728 and #1631: a quota that loosens, and external adapters on the instance's limiter (Opus implementer, 2026-10-22)

- **Reserved for Björn, ruled by implementer on Opus: the frozen-surface change to
  `crates/knobas-http/**`** (waived by Björn 2026-10-22). *Ruling:* private to `limiter.rs`
  behind the unchanged public `InstanceLimiter`; no signature, `HttpConfig` field or adapter
  changes. Booked in `docs/contract/10.8/1728-1631-knobas-http-quota-loosens-and-wasm-host-shares-it.md`.
  *Reversing:* low, one module.
- **#1728's "Ruled up front" section** (registration tokens, loosening when no live holder asks
  for the stricter quota, a drained limiter on loosening, a tightening as in #1630) is built as
  ruled. Nothing in the work showed it wrong.
- **When the quota is worked out again.** *Ruling:* only when a limiter for the origin is built,
  as the ticket says (the prune is in `for_origin`). A holder's drop does not loosen anything by
  itself, so a long-lived holder (Kuma's socket) stays at the stricter quota until the next run,
  read or flush builds a client for the origin, which is seconds to minutes in practice. A drop
  hook would need the registration to point back at its slot for a gain nobody would see.
  *Reversing:* low, a `Drop` on the registration.
- **A change that loosens one field and tightens the other.** *Ruling:* it counts as a loosening
  and starts drained. The burst it would hand out is the one the ticket forbids, and a drained
  limiter at a lower burst costs one refill. *Reversing:* low, one comparison.
- **Which of an external adapter's requests wait on the limiter.** The spec says the host awaits
  "the same limiter for the instance origin before each send". *Ruling:* requests for the
  instance only (the ones the credential goes on). A request to another host the manifest
  declares carries nothing of the reader's, so no account of theirs can be locked by it, and
  spending the instance's quota on it would slow the built-in clients for traffic that never
  reaches the instance. *Reversing:* low; pace those on their own origin's limiter.
- **The quota the host asks for.** *Ruling:* `HttpConfig::default()`'s rate and burst (5/s, 10),
  read from that, so no new public constant enters the frozen crate. *Reversing:* low.
- **What bounds the host's wait on the limiter.** *Ruling:* the call's deadline, not the
  component's connect and first-byte timeouts. Those bound the server's answer. A component with
  a short timeout would otherwise get an error for every request the pacing delays and, being
  naive, ask again at once. A wait that outlasted the deadline (it cannot: the deadline ends the
  call first) would reach the component as `connection-limit-reached`, logged on the host's side
  with the `LocalQuota` message. *Reversing:* low.
- **Where in `send` the wait sits.** *Ruling:* last before the request goes out, after the
  allowlist, the lookup guard and the buffered body, so a token is spent only on a request that
  leaves. *Reversing:* low.
- **How long the host's registration lives.** *Ruling:* as long as the built source's
  `net::Policy`. The registry builds a source per run, read and test, as it builds an
  `HttpClient`, so an external adapter's registration ages the same way. *Reversing:* low.
- **#1631's first criterion: "at most 10 arrive within the first second".** At the http crate's
  defaults (5/s, burst 10) a correct implementation lets 10 + 5 through in the first second, so
  the criterion cannot pass as worded. *Ruling:* the test asserts the burst (at most 10 within
  150 ms, under one 200 ms refill), all 30 arriving, and the last no sooner than 3.5 s after the
  first (twenty at five a second). The wording fix is filed as #1737 (`backlog`). *Reversing:*
  n/a.
- **#1729 (the write queue reads a limiter timeout as a refusal).** An external adapter's write
  never fails with `LocalQuota`: the host's wait is bounded by the call's deadline only. What it
  can do is spend some of that deadline waiting, and a call stopped at its deadline was already
  `Protocol` with no status before #1631, which the queue reads as a refusal. Reaching it through
  the limiter needs a wait as long as the manifest's deadline (default ten minutes, at least one
  second) behind a quota other clients are spending. *Ruling:* not reachable in practice, and the
  deadline half is #1729's question, not this PR's; said so on #1729. *Reversing:* n/a.

## #1728 and #1631: merge review of PR #1735 (Opus merge-manager, 2026-10-22)

- **Pacing only the requests for the instance.** #1618 says the host "awaits the same limiter for
  the instance origin before each send"; read alone, every send. *Ruling:* the implementer's
  reading stands and meets #1631's intent. The paced set is exactly the requests the host puts the
  credential on; A9 places the quota with the host because "the host attaches the credential and
  owns the socket", and #1631's failure is a lockout of the reader's account, which only the
  instance holds. The component never sees the secret, so a request to another declared host
  cannot spend the reader's account. *Reversing:* low, pace those on their own origin's limiter.
- **The quota is worked out again only when a limiter is built.** *Ruling:* accepted. #1728's
  first criterion holds (`a_quota_loosens_once_the_stricter_client_is_gone`). The reader cases hold
  because every source is built per run, flush, live read and test and dropped after
  (`scheduler::build_source`, the write queue, `crud.rs`); nothing caches a source or an
  `HttpClient` (#1618 rules a registry cache out of scope). The save-then-sync path is witnessed
  at the limiter seam, not end to end in the app: a run still in flight at the save keeps the old
  quota until a client is built after it ends. Kuma's process-long socket asks for 25/50, so a Kuma
  source set above 25/s stays capped at 25, no worse than before; #1723 owns the socket.
  *Reversing:* low.
- **A change looser in one field and stricter in the other is a loosening.** *Ruling:* accepted;
  it costs one refill and hands out no burst. *Reversing:* low.
- **The host's wait is bounded by the call's deadline only.** *Ruling:* accepted. `limits::bounded`
  drops the whole call at the deadline, wait included
  (`the_deadline_stops_a_call_waiting_on_the_limiter`); the component's timeouts start after the
  wait and bound the server's answer. *Reversing:* low.
- **#1631's "at most 10 within the first second".** *Ruling:* the substituted test is honest. At
  5/s and burst 10 a correct limiter lets about 15 through in the first second; at most 10 within
  150 ms bounds the burst, a spread of at least 3.5 s for 30 bounds the rate, and before the change
  all 30 came within 150 ms. Criterion ticked with that note; #1737 fixes the wording.
- **A tightening after a loosening hands out a fresh burst.** Two sources at 5/10 and 10/20 whose
  clients alternate get A's burst of 10 on every B→A turn, which #1630's monotone quota never
  did. #1728 rules that "a tightening keeps #1630's behaviour", so the PR follows the ticket; the
  gap matters only for turns shorter than about burst/rate seconds. Filed as #1740 (`backlog`).
  *Reversing:* n/a.

### #1632: bring-up and shutdown a test can drive (Opus, 2026-10-22)

- **`bring_up`'s arguments.** *Fork:* the ticket writes `bring_up(handle, profile)`; the database
  URL comes from `KNOBAS_DB_URL` and the registry from `Registry::for_process()`, neither of which a
  test can point elsewhere. *Ruling:* `bring_up(handle, profile, db_url, registry)`.
  `spawn_bring_up` passes the environment variable and the process registry; a test passes its
  scratch database's URL and a registry of its own. Setting the variable is `unsafe` in edition
  2024 and reaches every concurrent test in the binary, and a fixture adapter loaded into the
  process registry would show up in every other test's adapter list. The `for_process` scan's
  allowed bring-up site moves from `sources/mod.rs` to `lib.rs`. *Reversing:* low.
- **The profile travels as an argument.** *Ruling:* `sources::start` and `backup::start` take the
  `&Profile` bring-up was given instead of each reading it from managed state, so a bring-up runs
  on one profile throughout. *Reversing:* low.
- **The retry test uses two mock apps over one registry.** *Fork:* bring up one app twice, or two
  apps. *Ruling:* two apps. A retry follows a failure, and `sources::start` manages its state last,
  so on a retry the first attempt's sources state was never managed. What the retry inherits is
  the registry. Bringing one app up twice would leave the second scheduler orphaned, since Tauri
  keeps the first `manage` and the scheduler never stops. *Reversing:* low.
- **The "recording stub scheduler" is the real scheduler over a recording adapter.** *Fork:*
  `SourcesState` holds a concrete `knobas_sync::Scheduler`, so a stub scheduler would need a trait
  over it, a second scheduler surface. *Ruling:* the shutdown test starts the real scheduler with
  one adapter whose sync parks until it is dropped, and the drop records whether the application
  pool (the one `shutdown_database` closes) was closed yet. Swapping the two calls makes it record
  `true`. *Reversing:* low.
- **`grep -c 'include_str!' wiring.rs` is 0 cannot pass.** The file holds eight more `include_str!`
  scans (plugin registration, the handler list, plugin version pins) that order nothing and that
  the spec does not retire. The two byte-offset tests are gone; the criterion is ticked with that
  note, and the wording fix is a follow-up. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **The suggestion-pass scan's replacement witnesses the handover, not the count.** *Ruling:* a
  mock source synced through the scheduler bring-up started proposes links, and the mutant that
  takes the pass off the scheduler fails it. "Built exactly once" cannot be seen from outside the
  process. Since #1611, nothing but the scheduler holds a pass. *Reversing:* low.
- **`replace` drops a recorded update check.** *Ruling:* acceptable. `sources::start` re-runs the
  check in the background on every bring-up, a retry included. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **Merge-manager: the declarations come from bring-up's registry, not the `Lifecycle`'s.**
  *Fork:* the two could differ, and Settings reads the `Lifecycle`'s. *Ruling:* accepted. Both
  production callers of `spawn_bring_up` (`setup` and `retry_database`) pass
  `Registry::for_process()`, and `setup` manages `Lifecycle::new()`, which is the same list;
  `bring_up` with any other registry exists only behind `test-util`. *Reversing:* low.
- **Merge-manager: the `include_str!` criterion's intent is met.** *Ruling:* both byte-offset
  tests are gone and their claims run in `tests/it/bring_up.rs`; the eight scans left in
  `wiring.rs` pin plugin registration, the handler list and version pins, and order nothing. The
  tick with a note stands; #1738 (backlog) rewords the criterion. *Reversing:* n/a.
## #1628: a write refused its credential waits for a new one; an unreachable one climbs the ladder (implementer, Opus)
## #1628: a write whose credential was rejected waits for a new one; an unreachable one climbs the ladder (implementer, Opus)

### What clears the wait for a source with both a secret and an account

**The fork:** Kuma stores an API key (its reads) and an account (its writes) in one keychain entry, saved by one `set_source_secret`. Release on the half the writes use, or on any save?

**Ruling:** any save through `set_source_secret` releases the source's `unauthorized` writes: the secret, the account, or both, whatever the connection test answers afterwards. The form cannot show which half changed (absent means keep, #452), Kuma's test reads with the key and never logs in with the account, and a test that fails leaves the health needing a human, which the tick skips anyway.

**Cost of reversing:** low. One call in `crud::set_secret`.

### A source edit of its address or configuration releases too

**The fork:** a write whose adapter would not build (a configuration the adapter refuses) waits as `unauthorized`, the "a person has to act" reason. With the tick no longer re-sending those, fixing the configuration would leave the write waiting until *Flush now*.

**Ruling:** `crud::update` releases when the patch carries `base_url` or `config`. A rename, an interval or the enable switch releases nothing. This adds a release the ticket does not list; it contradicts nothing, because it is a person acting, never the tick.

**Cost of reversing:** low. One condition in `crud::update`.

### A release clears `wait_reason`; no activity line, no migration

**The fork:** how a released row is told apart from a refused one: a new column or timestamp, or the reason itself.

**Ruling:** `release_unauthorized` sets `wait_reason = null` and keeps `detail` and `attempted_at`. The flush loop reads null as owed. The panel reads "Waiting." until the next flush sends it: one tick, or, where the connection test after a save failed and left the health needing a human, until that health clears or the reader presses *Flush now*. A release writes no activity line: the attempt after it does (`waiting` again if refused, `sent` if not).

**Cost of reversing:** medium. A column would need a migration.

### A 401 that answered a replaced credential is not recorded

**The fork:** a credential saved while a flush is in flight: the 401 that comes back was the answer to the old credential, and recording it would re-reason the released row `unauthorized` with nothing left to release it.

**Ruling:** a per-source change count, process-wide beside the flush lock. `knobas_sync::write_queue::release_unauthorized` bumps it, and the flush reads it before building its adapter. `waited` skips recording an `unauthorized` whose count moved, holding the count across its statement so a change lands wholly before or after. The credential save never waits for an in-flight flush. Worst case: one extra attempt with the new credential.

**Cost of reversing:** low. Removing it brings back the race.

### The ladder's rung is the row's `attempts`; the clock is the process's

**The fork:** the sync side counts consecutive failed runs. A write row has `attempts`, which also counts a hold that was released.

**Ruling:** `attempts` is the rung, `config::backoff_after` the ladder, `Utc::now()` against the database-stamped `attempted_at` the clock. The embedded server runs on the same host (ADR-0001). A write that was held, released and then failed starts a rung or two higher. That is acceptable for a write that has already failed more than once.

**Cost of reversing:** low.

### *Flush now* skips nothing, once

**The fork:** whether *Flush now* for every source still skips a source whose health needs a human, and whether its later passes also ignore the waits.

**Ruling:** it skips no source and ignores every wait on its first pass only. Later passes, which let an entity's next write follow one that just landed, use the tick's test, so a press sends each unauthorized write at most once. A press is the reader asking. The lockout risk is one request per press.

**Cost of reversing:** low.

### `write_queue_flush_all.rs` moves to scratch databases

**The fork:** a sibling test's `flush_all` fails to build this file's sources (its secret store lacks their credential) and records `unauthorized`. That used to last one tick; now it lasts for good.

**Ruling:** each test there takes `scratch_database`, as `background_write.rs` does.

**Cost of reversing:** low.

## #1628: merge review of PR #1736 (Opus merge-manager, 2026-10-22)

The implementer's seven rulings above stand, the `update_source` release beyond the ticket included: a person edits the address or configuration, and the tick never releases anything on its own.

### A live run is owed, and `just kuma-live` is it

**The fork:** the PR changes no adapter, only the write queue, which lives in `knobas-sync`. The working model's live-run rule names "the sync engine", and its re-run list names `knobas-sync`.

**Ruling:** owed. `knobas-sync` is on the re-run list. `just kuma-live` drives the queue end to end (`kuma_write_live`: submit, flush, mirror re-read) and covers the Kuma path that #1627's `Unconfirmed` waits sit on. It needs no JVM product. It ran green on the rebased head `5527b61b`: 14, 3 and 1 passed.

**Cost of reversing:** none. It is a run, not a change.

### `write_queue_flush_all.rs`'s scratch databases are test isolation, not a hidden leak

**The fork:** whether giving each test its own database hides a real cross-source fault in `flush_all`.

**Ruling:** it does not. The leak needed two tests' sources in one database, with a `flush_all` that holds one test's registry and secret store but iterates every source. In the app there is one registry and one secret store for every source, so a sibling's build failure cannot happen there. Each source still has its own gate and its own errors, and `a_source_that_cannot_write_does_not_stop_another_source` still pins that.

**Cost of reversing:** low.

### A refusal skipped as stale can go once more inside the same flush

**The fork:** `waited` leaves a stale 401's row released. If another write of the source lands in the same pass, the loop's next pass finds the released row owed. It sends it again with the adapter built before the save, so with the old credential.

**Ruling:** accepted, no change. It needs one source's credential to be refused for one write and accepted for another in the same flush, which a single credential does not do. The extra sends are bounded by the writes that land in that flush. The next flush builds with the new credential.

**Cost of reversing:** low. One check of the count between passes.

### A keychain fault during a flush waits for a person now; follow-up, not fixed here

**The fork:** `build` maps `RunFailure::Secret` to `unauthorized`. A locked macOS keychain lands there (`SecretError::Backend`). Since this PR, that write waits for a person, while the sync side climbs the ladder for the same failure.

**Ruling:** not fixed in this PR. The classification predates it. Both fixes cost more than the review: `unreachable` mislabels the panel, and a new reason needs a migration. Re-entering the credential, which the panel's "The credential was rejected." leads to, releases the write, and so does *Flush now*. Filed as #1741 (`ready-for-agent`).

**Cost of reversing:** low.

### The ladder reads the row the way the sync side reads its log

The write side's rung is `attempts`, 1 after the first failure. That is the sync side's `failures_since_last_ok`, 1 after the first failed run. Both go through `config::backoff_after`, so the first retry comes at 60 s on both. #1627's `Unconfirmed` on a resend-harmless write classifies `unreachable` and is spaced by this ladder. #1630's limiter `Protocol { status: None }` still settles a write refused (`retryable`), untouched here and never on the ladder. That stays #1729 (backlog).

## #1674 — reset every module-level store between tests

- **Store imports in `test-resets.ts`.** *Fork:* import the stores at the top, or inside each
  reset. *Ruling:* inside each reset, skipping a store a file's partial `vi.mock` stops from
  loading (`[vitest] No "x" export`). The setup file runs before a test file registers its
  mocks, so a top-level import loaded the real `ipc/app` and broke about sixty tests.
  *Reversing:* low.
- **Scope.** *Fork:* reset all 33 module-level stores or the six the ticket names. *Ruling:* the
  six; the rest sit in `NOT_YET_RESET`, which the completeness test accepts and #1743 empties.
  *Reversing:* low.
- **Unwitnessed resets (merge-manager).** The implementer left `health.reset`'s `phase` and
  `kindRegistry.reset`'s `loaded` unwitnessed. *Ruling:* a test each is owed, since both are
  one-liners on a store factory; added to `test-resets.test.ts`, both mutants now die. *Reversing:* low.
- **Scope against the ticket (merge-manager).** *Fork:* does six resets plus a 19-entry
  `NOT_YET_RESET` meet "a new store without a reset is red"? *Ruling:* yes. The ticket names
  six stores and all six reset; the list is a known-gaps list, and a store in neither list is red
  (test 1), a list entry that is gone or reset is red (test 2, which also fails if the scan finds
  no files). #1743 empties it. *Reversing:* low.
- **Skipped stores (merge-manager).** `resetStores` swallows only `[vitest] No "x" export`; a
  store a file's partial mock stops from loading is not in that file's graph, so it holds no state

## #1676 Build every job address from the entity id

- **Week row has no kind.** *Fork:* a Week target carries an entity id and no kind, so a page or
  repo cannot be told from a ticket. *Ruling:* read the kind with `getEntity` once per id and link
  through `entityAddress(kind, id, true)`; until it answers, or if it fails, draw plain text. No IPC
  change, §10.8 untouched. *Reversing:* low; a `kind` on the week row would drop the read.
- **Old ticket bookmarks.** *Ruling:* `#/ticket/<id>` and the `#/entity/<id>` resolver now land on
  `#/job/<entity id>` (the job page reads both forms since #1476). *Reversing:* low.
- **Week link appears after the kind read (merge-manager).** *Fork:* the key is plain text for
  the moment the read takes, which the ticket's "No visual change" line does not name. *Ruling:*
  accepted; `just shot` of `#/time/week` under `?fake-ipc`, before and after a 1.5 s settle, shows
  the same table and the same underlined keys. The reads are cached per entity id (`asked`, kept
  across weeks), so a re-render issues none; a failed read is retried on the next render. No
  follow-up for a `kind` on the week row: three reads a week, once each. *Reversing:* low.
## #1639 — read back a keychain secret that holds a quote, a backslash or a tab

Ruled 2026-10-22 by the implementer on Opus. Spec #1620, ruling C1 (owned `String`s, no v3).

- **Where the round trip runs.** *Fork:* the ticket wants a test "through `put` then `get`" that is
  red before the fix, but `MemoryStore` keeps the `Secret` itself and never encodes, so it cannot
  go red; `KeyringStore` encodes, but its only round-trip test writes to the real keychain.
  *Ruling:* a `#[cfg(test)]` constructor, `KeyringStore::over`, hands the store
  `keyring_core::mock::Store`, the in-memory credential store `keyring-core` ships (no new
  dependency). `put` and `get` then run their real `encode`/`decode` path and no keychain is
  opened. `MemoryStore` is left as it is: making it store the envelope would change what every
  `knobas-app` test runs against, which is a separate ticket. *Reversing:* low; one test
  constructor and four tests.
- **"The same escapes round-trip in `kind`".** *Fork:* knobas writes `kind` only from four fixed
  names, so no quote, backslash or tab can round-trip in it. *Ruling:* read it as the reader's
  half: a stored item whose kind is spelled with a JSON escape (`api\u005ftoken`) reads as that
  kind, which is the case the borrowed field refused. *Reversing:* low.
## #1635: put the bookkeeping rows back when a restore fails

Ruled 2026-10-22 by the implementer on Opus, inside spec #1619's ruling B3 (snapshot and re-insert).

- **Snapshot all four bookkeeping tables, not only the ones the archive carries.** *Fork:* the
  ticket says "reads the bookkeeping rows"; the clears touch only the carried tables. *Ruling:*
  read all four. Clearing `dep_layer` cascades into `dep_layer_kind`, so a partial archive that
  carries `dep_layer` alone still empties a table the restore never names. *Reversing:* low.
- **The put-back clears each table before it inserts, in one transaction.** *Ruling:* a share
  export carries no `setting` or `dep_view`, so those rows were never cleared, and inserting the
  snapshot on top of them collides on the primary key. Children are cleared first and parents
  inserted first, so `dep_layer_kind` finds its layer. Witnessed by the partial-archive test.
  *Reversing:* low.
- **The put-back runs before the rename shim's fold-up, and its own error wins.** *Fork:* the
  ticket says "returns the load error after the recovery" and does not say what happens when the
  recovery fails. *Ruling:* a failed put-back or fold-up returns its `sqlx` error, as the fold-up
  already did before this change. Rows lost here have no way back from the UI; a shim column left
  by a failed fold-up is dropped by the next restore. So the rows go first. *Reversing:* low.
- **The snapshot is `to_jsonb` text read back through `jsonb_populate_recordset`.** *Ruling:* no
  column list in Rust, so a column a later migration adds is carried with no edit, and no new
  dependency (`serde_json` is optional in `knobas-db`). *Reversing:* low.

Merge-manager review of #1745, on Opus:

- **A put-back that fails names the load's error too.** *Fork:* the implementer returned the
  put-back's bare `sqlx` error in place of the load's. *Ruling:* a new `BackupError::NotPutBack
  { load, source }` whose message says the restore failed, why, and that putting the settings
  and Dependencies layers back failed after it. That is the one outcome where rows are gone, so
  the user is told both. It reaches the UI as `internal`, the code every other restore failure
  already gets, so no IPC shape changes. A fold-up failure still returns its own error: a
  leftover shim column loses nothing. *Reversing:* low.
- **The archive's table of contents is read once, before anything is cleared.** *Fork:* the
  clears called `pg_restore --list` once per bookkeeping table, so a listing that failed after
  the first clear returned with no put-back. *Ruling:* one `carried_bookkeeping` call before the
  snapshot. A failed `delete` or `alter table` between the clears and the load still returns
  without a put-back; that is a statement on a local server that just answered, and wrapping it
  would need a partial-shim fold-up for no witnessed case. *Reversing:* low.
- **A put-back that cannot reconnect after a failed load is accepted, no follow-up.** *Ruling:*
  the rows are lost only when the embedded server stops answering in the moment between a failed
  `pg_restore` and the reconnect; before #1635 they were lost on every failed load. A durable
  snapshot (a scratch table or database) costs more than that window. *Reversing:* medium.
- **The `jsonb` round trip holds for every column these tables have.** `text`, `integer`,
  `boolean`, `jsonb` and `timestamptz` (microseconds kept), none nullable, no identity or
  generated column and no trigger; the tests compare `to_jsonb` text, timestamps included.
