## #1790 + #1795: bash-guard, in-place flags, arithmetic, function bodies, heredoc bodies (Opus implementer, 2026-10-23)

- **The perl class is the ticket's sketch plus `f` and `S`.** *Fork:* `[aclnpstuwTUWX0-9]` as
  sketched, or every perl flag that takes no argument. *Ruling:* `^-[aclfnpsStTuUwWX0-9]*i`.
  *Reasoning:* `-f` and `-S` take no argument, so `-fi` and `-Si` are in-place bundles too. `-C`
  stays out: `i` is one of its own letters (`-Ci`, a UTF-8 input layer). So do `-x`, `-d` and `-D`,
  which take a glued argument. *Reversing:* one character class.
- **BSD sed's `-I` counts as in place.** *Fork:* match only `-i`, or `-I` as well. *Ruling:* both,
  `^-[nErsuzal]*[iI]`. *Reasoning:* macOS `/usr/bin/sed -I '' s/a/b/ f` edits `f` in place
  (checked), and the old pattern let it write `~/.bashrc`. GNU sed has no `-I`, so the only cost
  there is refusing a command that errors anyway. *Reversing:* one letter.
- **`--in-place` matches its abbreviations down to `--i`.** *Fork:* the full word only, or its
  prefixes too. *Ruling:* its prefixes. *Reasoning:* GNU sed's
  getopt_long accepts any unambiguous prefix, and no other GNU sed long option starts with `i`.
  Not checked against a real GNU sed: none is installed on this machine. BSD sed has no long
  options. *Reversing:* one regex.
- **A `((` is arithmetic only when its inner group is closed by `))`.** *Fork:* every `((` at a
  command's start, or the shell's rule. *Ruling:* the shell's rule, for `((` and `$((` alike.
  *Reasoning:* bash 5.3 runs `((echo hi); echo there)` as two subshells and `echo $((echo a); echo
  b)` as a command substitution (checked). Reading those as arithmetic would hide their commands,
  and the old `$((` reader did hide them: `echo $((cd x); ls)` passed. *Reversing:* two lines in
  `arithmetic`.
- **A substitution inside arithmetic is parsed.** *Fork:* keep `$((...))` opaque, as #1791 had it,
  or parse its `$(...)` and backquotes. *Ruling:* parse them. *Reasoning:* the shell runs them, and
  `echo $(( $(cd x && pwd) + 1 ))` passed. Same direction as the ticket: it only turns a hidden
  command into a seen one. *Reversing:* one line.
- **"A command's start" for `((`.** *Fork:* any `((` with no word open, or only where a command
  can start. *Ruling:* no word yet, or only reserved words, `for`, `time`, `time -p` and `coproc`
  before it (`if ((x))`, `for ((i=0; ...))`, `time -p ((x))`). *Reasoning:* anywhere else `((` is
  a syntax error and nothing runs. *Reversing:* one set.
- **A heredoc body's substitutions join the heredoc's command as one word.** *Fork:* a command of
  their own, or a word of the command that opened the heredoc. *Ruling:* a word, with the text
  `<<DELIM`, never the substitution's text. *Reasoning:* that is where the shell runs them, so
  `cd <<EOF` keeps its own-argument exemption the way `cd "$(...)"` does, and a `$(cat
  ./.git/HEAD)` in the body of `tee /tmp/x <<EOF` is not read as a write target. A delimiter
  holding any quote or backslash makes the body data, as in the shell. *Reversing:* low.
- **A `((` that is no arithmetic leaves no heredoc pending (Opus merge-manager, review finding).**
  *Fork:* fix in this PR, or file a follow-up. *Ruling:* fix here: `arithmetic` restores
  `self.pending` when it returns None. *Reasoning:* the caller reads the same text again as a
  substitution or subshell, so a `<<EOF` inside it was registered twice and the second "body"
  swallowed the lines after the real one: `echo $(( $(cat <<EOF) ); ls)`, `body`, `EOF`,
  `cd x && y` passed, where `main` refused it and bash runs `cd x && y`. The PR introduced the
  second reading, so it closes it; two tests pin it. *Reversing:* three lines.

Transcript replay, a measurement rather than a ruling: all Bash commands in this project's
transcripts and their subagent transcripts, 61,185 unique (66,603 calls), old guard (61a7dd73)
against new: 0 verdicts differ, 0 exceptions; both refuse 23,427. So no doc tells an agent to type
a newly refused command, and no doc changes. The merge-manager's re-run on the fixed head, against
`main`'s guard: 61,334 unique, 0 verdicts differ, 0 exceptions, none slower than 50 ms.
### #1789: a silent port beside a live pid (Opus implementer, 2026-10-23)

- **Does a free owner lock plus a silent port clear the lock with a live recorded pid?** Reserved
  for Björn, ruled by implementer on Opus, under Björn's 2026-10-22 waiver for spec #1619's
  reserved steps. It reverses the rest of ruling B5. *Ruling:* yes. `inspect_lock` reads the port
  alone, and `Lock::LiveProcess` and its `AlreadyRunning` are gone. *Reasoning:* the ticket's case
  against, a postmaster of ours starting or in crash recovery whose knobas died, never reaches this
  arm, because such a postmaster answers on its port. Where one could reach it, clearing costs one
  failed start and no data. Evidence, from PostgreSQL 18.6 on this Mac (`postgres -D <scratch> -p
  <port> -c listen_addresses=127.0.0.1`, a cluster of 3 to 6 million committed rows crashed with
  `kill -9`; the scripts are `issue-1789-e*.py` in that run's scratchpad):
  1. **Crash recovery answers.** The postmaster logs `listening on IPv4 address "127.0.0.1"` before
     its startup process logs `database system was interrupted`. With the startup process frozen
     (`SIGSTOP`) mid-redo, a TCP handshake on the recorded port succeeds and `psql` gets `FATAL:
     the database system is not yet accepting connections` (57P03). That is `Lock::Live`, and
     `adopt` refuses it as `cannot connect on port <n>`, as before this PR.
  2. **Shutdown answers.** With the checkpointer frozen in a fast shutdown, `postmaster.pid` reads
     `stopping`, and the port still answers (`the database system is shutting down`) until exit.
  3. **The silent window is 2 ms.** Over 20 starts, from `postmaster.pid` naming a pid and port to
     the port answering: min 2.08, median 2.22, max 2.46 ms. In PostgreSQL 18 the order is lock
     file, shared memory, bind. A relaunch, which first runs `setup()` and `pg_ctl start`, cannot
     land in it unless the postmaster is frozen there. The other way a postmaster of ours is
     silent on `127.0.0.1` is an orphan an older build started on `localhost` that kept only
     `::1` (#1775, evidence 1). Today that one is a lockout until it is killed by hand.
  4. **Clearing under recovery.** `postmaster.pid` removed under the recovering postmaster of (1):
     a second postmaster is refused with `pre-existing shared memory block (key …) is still in
     use`. 65 s later the first logs `performing immediate shutdown because data directory lock
     file is invalid`, then `issuing SIGKILL to recalcitrant children` and `database system is
     shut down`, leaving no process and no SysV segment. The next start logs `database system was
     interrupted while in recovery`, replays from the same redo point, and is ready in 1.4 s.
     PostgreSQL adds its generic hint `This probably means that some data is corrupted`, but all
     6,000,000 rows and the marker row are there, and `pg_amcheck --heapallindexed` exits 0.
     Redo is idempotent, so an interrupted crash recovery just runs again.
  5. **Clearing a postmaster frozen after shared memory, before bind** (pid and port written,
     port silent): the second postmaster is refused by the interlock as in (4). The first, once
     resumed, binds, recovers and serves without a lock file (it logs `could not open file
     "postmaster.pid"`), until the minute check of (4) stops it; this run killed it first.
  6. **Clearing a postmaster frozen before shared memory** (pid and port written, port silent,
     no segment, so exactly the old `Lock::LiveProcess`): the second postmaster wins the
     interlock, replays and reaches `ready`. The first, resumed, exits on the interlock, and its
     exit unlinks `postmaster.pid`, which is now the second's (PostgreSQL removes its lock-file
     path unconditionally on exit). The second keeps serving and shuts itself down 56 to 60 s later
     (`lock file is invalid`). In a knobas window, #1779's watch sees the missing file within 5 s
     and the window goes `failed`. *Retry* is refused by the interlock until that shutdown, then
     starts. Only one startup process ever ran: rows, marker and `pg_amcheck` all clean on the
     final start, in all three runs.
  So clearing never puts two servers on the files, and its worst case (6, which needs a frozen
  postmaster) is a window that fails once and recovers on *Retry*. Keeping the lock costs a
  lockout on every launch until the reader deletes `postmaster.pid`: the recycled pid after a
  reboot, and the `::1` orphan, which only clearing gets rid of. A ps-name check (clear only when
  the live pid is not a `postgres`) was considered and rejected: a recycled pid can land on a
  second profile's or Homebrew's postgres, and that lockout would stay. *Reversing:* one `if` in
  `inspect_lock` and the variant.
- **§10.8.** *Ruling:* booked (`docs/contract/10.8/1789-a-silent-port-clears-a-live-pids-lock.md`):
  the boot screen's `postmaster.pid records process <pid>, which is still running, but nothing
  answers…` refusal is gone. No type changes. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **No test pins the recovering postmaster's refusal.** *Ruling:* not added. Freezing a startup
  process from a cargo test needs a crashed cluster and `SIGSTOP` on a child the test did not
  spawn. The arm it reaches, `Lock::Live` into `adopt`, is unchanged here and keeps its tests.
  *Reversing:* n/a.

### #1789: merge-manager review (Opus merge-manager, 2026-10-23)

- **The implementer's ruling (a silent port clears the lock whatever the pid does).** Reserved for
  Björn, ruled by merge-manager on Opus as well: confirmed. *Reasoning:* the logs bear out each
  step. In the recovery run the postmaster logged `listening on IPv4 address "127.0.0.1"` before
  `database system was interrupted`, and `psql` got 57P03 during redo. A 57P03 is a
  `sqlx::Error::Database` whose code does not start with `28`, so `adopt` refuses it and does not
  read it as a stranger. With the lock cleared under it, the second postmaster got `pre-existing
  shared memory block ... is still in use`. In the ordering where the frozen postmaster had not yet
  created shared memory, the interlock fired the other way round: the new server removed the
  crashed run's unattached segment and created its own, and the frozen one, once resumed, got the
  same FATAL on the new server's segment and never reached redo. Only one startup process wrote,
  and the rows, marker and `pg_amcheck` were clean. The *2 ms* window is measured
  (`issue-1789-e3-window.py`), but on an idle machine. Re-run by the merge-manager during a cargo
  build, twice 20 starts: min 1.67 and 2.34, median 2.72 and 3.97, max 34.57 and 33.99 ms. So the
  `inspect_lock` docs say "a few milliseconds". The argument never depended on the width, because
  the interlock is the guard. The §10.8 entry now also covers the pre-shared-memory ordering, where
  the launch reaches `ready` and #1779's watch then fails it. *Reversing:* as the implementer's.
- **Mutant M4 (a silent port read as answering) survives the integration test.** *Ruling:* no
  integration case owed. At `EmbeddedDb::start` the mutant is equivalent: `adopt` takes the refused
  connect as a stranger, `launch` clears the lock and calls `start_managed` again, and that start
  succeeds without reaching `inspect_lock`. Nothing at that seam can tell the two paths apart. The
  unit test pins which path is taken. *Reversing:* low.
- **No test pins a recovering postmaster's refusal.** *Ruling:* not owed by this PR. That arm
  (`Lock::Live` into `adopt`, 57P03 into `AlreadyRunning`) is unchanged here, and constructing a
  `PgDatabaseError` with a chosen code needs a live server in that state. *Reversing:* low.
## #1797: a submit flushes its own entity (Opus implementer, 2026-10-23)

- **Which of the ticket's two directions.** *Fork:* the submit's flush tries its own entity and
  leaves the rest of the source to the flush task, or a flusher that finds the source's lock taken
  leaves the writes it has not reached to the holder. *Ruling:* the first. *Reasoning:* the holder
  read its writes before the submit queued, and on a failing source its pass makes no progress, so
  it never re-reads and never reaches the new write. The second direction would leave a person's
  write untried until the next tick, which is the opposite of "returns once its own write has been
  tried", and it makes what a submit sends depend on who held the lock. The first changes one
  filter on `due`, keeps the per-write lock and its re-read (#1629), the quota watch around each
  write (#1729), the ladder (#1628) and per-entity order. *Reversing:* the filter.
- **How far into the entity.** *Fork:* stop at the submitted write, or follow the entity's writes
  as far as they go, as the source-wide flush did. *Ruling:* as far as they go. *Reasoning:* a
  write queued behind it on the same entity was blocked by it, and *Send mine anyway* on a held
  head is expected to let its successors follow (story 22's
  `one_entitys_writes_keep_their_order_without_blocking_another` asks for exactly that). The cost
  is one entity's later writes, not the source's. *Reversing:* an `id <=` bound in the filter.
- **Which callers narrow.** *Ruling:* `submit`, `apply_anyway`, `amend` and a new
  `flush_entity_of(deps, id)`, which the app's `flush` (every `submit_write`, `log_work` and
  background send) now calls in place of `flush_source`. `flush_source`, the flush task and
  *Flush now* still reach the whole source. *Reasoning:* the ticket names the submit, *Send mine
  anyway* and an amend; the app's send is the same submit by another door. A press of *Flush now*
  asks for the whole source. *Reversing:* low.
- **The timing test's clock.** *Ruling:* it starts when the first slow write goes on the wire, as
  the fake records it, not when the submit is called, and the fake dwells per entity so the
  submit's own write takes no time. *Reasoning:* timed from the submit, the old code returns at
  2 × D minus however late the submit started, which can fall under the bound; timed from the
  first send it cannot, since both sleeps run in full after it. D is 1 s so the DB work of a submit
  under load stays far under the other D of headroom. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **A §10.8 entry.** *Ruling:* booked (`1797-a-submit-flushes-its-own-entity.md`): a submit no
  longer sends the other owed writes of its source, which a caller of `submit_write` can observe.
  *Reversing:* one file.

### #1797 merge-manager review (Opus, 2026-10-23)

- **The 1 s timing headroom.** *Fork:* widen the four timing tests to an event or barrier, or keep
  `2 * DWELL`. *Ruling:* keep it. *Reasoning:* the clock starts when the first slow write goes on
  the wire, so the database work under load falls inside the second `DWELL`, not the first. Ten
  runs of the four beside two full `cargo test -p knobas-sync` runs, at a load average of 24 to 46,
  all passed. *Reversing:* low, a test-only change.
- **A submit behind a head another flusher just sent.** *Fork:* fix in this PR, or file it.
  *Ruling:* file it (#1807, backlog). *Reasoning:* a submit on E whose earlier write another
  flusher is sending finds that write `Gone` and counts no progress, so it returns without trying
  its own. The write is not stranded, because the sending flusher re-reads `heads` after its round.
  The loop already did this on a source with one entity, and it changes `flush`'s progress rule for
  every caller, which is outside #1797. *Reversing:* the follow-up.
- **A submit on a source that needs a person.** *Ruling:* not owed. A submit there no longer
  tries the other entities' untried writes. The tick skips such a source (#1628) and sends them
  once it answers again, and the submit's own try would have failed the same way. *Reversing:* n/a.
## #1807: a submit behind a head another flusher just sent (Opus implementer, 2026-10-23)

- **What a closed head gives the flusher that waited for it.** *Fork:* count it as progress, so
  `flush` re-reads `heads` after the pass, or hand the turn, lock and all, to the entity's next
  write. *Ruling:* hand the turn on (`turn`). *Reasoning:* the ticket asks for the submit's write
  to go before the other entity's slow write is done. Counting progress drops the lock between the
  re-read and the next `turn`, and the flush task, queued on the FIFO mutex behind the submit,
  takes it for its other write first. The submit then still waits a whole send. Handing on keeps
  the lock and re-reads the entity's head under it, so per-entity order, #1729's quota watch
  (inside `attempt`) and #1628's ladder (`heads` filters `owed`) are unchanged. The successor is
  read under the lock, so no flusher sends it twice. *Reversing:* one `if` in `turn`.
- **Which closed heads hand on.** *Fork:* only `sent`, or every closed state. *Ruling:* `sent` and
  `discarded` (`!is_open()`). *Reasoning:* either one makes the entity's next write its head, as
  `store::due` reads it. A `held` or `refused` head still blocks the entity, so `heads` returns
  nothing for it, and a head another flusher attempted and failed is still pending with
  `attempted_at` moved, which stays `Gone`, as the ticket's second criterion requires. *Reversing:*
  the predicate.
- **The flush task and *Flush now* follow the same rule.** *Ruling:* yes, it is in `turn`, which
  every pass uses. *Reasoning:* a task waiting for a head a submit just landed now sends that
  entity's next write in the same turn, not on its next pass. That is still one write of that
  entity, in queue order, and the successor is never one the task's own list held, since `due`
  gives one write per entity. On a *Flush now* the successor is read without the `owed` filter, as
  every head of that pass is. It cannot be waiting anything out anyway: a write is attempted only
  as its entity's head. *Reversing:* pass a reach to `turn`.
- **The timing test reads rows, not a clock.** *Ruling:* the submit starts once the head is on the
  wire, and the test reads its own write's state and the other entity's write's state the moment it
  returns: `sent` and `pending`. *Reasoning:* the other entity's write takes 1 s after the submit
  lets go of the lock. That leaves one `heads` query of headroom, not a share of a bound, and a
  loaded machine cannot push the old code under it. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **The withdrawn case is withdrawn mid-send.** *Ruling:* through the fake's
  `Interrupt::Withdraw`, which fires at the end of the head's dwell, once the submit is waiting for
  the source. *Reasoning:* the first draft withdrew it before the submit, so the submit read the
  next write as its head straight away and the test passed on the old code too (mutants M1 and M3
  survived it). *Reversing:* n/a.
- **A §10.8 entry.** *Ruling:* booked (`1807-a-submit-behind-a-landed-head-tries-its-own-write.md`):
  `submit_write` now finds its write `sent` and asks for the mirror refresh where it used to skip
  it. *Reversing:* one file.
- **The ladder on a handed-on write (merge-manager on Opus, PR #1812).** *Fork:* leave the hand-on's
  `owed` filter unpinned, as the implementer's ruling argued a successor cannot be waiting, or pin
  it. *Ruling:* pin it, with `a_head_withdrawn_while_the_task_waited_hands_on_only_to_an_owed_write`.
  *Reasoning:* a successor can be waiting after all: a flusher reads the head, the reader withdraws
  it while the flusher waits for the lock, and a second flusher tries the successor, now the head,
  and records `unreachable`. The mutant that reads the hand-on with `Pass::Now` survived every
  existing test and sent that write before its rung; the new test kills it. *Reversing:* delete
  the test.

## #1638: a panicked run is recorded by the closing guard (Opus implementer, 2026-10-23)

- **How the guard records from a `Drop`.** *Fork:* `catch_unwind` around the run, a STATUS
  bound on old open rows (the ticket's second fix direction), or the guard spawning the run's
  tail. *Ruling:* the guard hands `Inner::end_run` (the tail of `run_task`, factored out) to the
  scheduler's `Background` set with an `error` verdict. *Reasoning:* spec #1619 says the closing
  guard records the ending, and the guard is what also sees a task dropped without a panic.
  `Background::spawn` is synchronous and refuses once the quit has begun, so the quit's abort
  keeps today's behaviour (watchers closed at once, the row left to `reconcile_abandoned`) and
  `shutdown` awaits a spawned tail under the grace. A STATUS bound would leave the row open and
  no ending emitted, which spec #1619 says must exist. *Reversing:* low.
- **Once, not twice.** *Fork:* disarm the guard's recording before `run_task`'s own `end_run`,
  or after it. *Ruling:* before: `run_task` clears the guard's `recorder` the moment it has a
  verdict. *Reasoning:* disarmed after, a task aborted or panicking inside `end_run` would have
  its row written and its `sync:state` ending sent a second time. Disarmed before, it gets only
  the watchers' ending, as it did before #1638. The spawned tail carries a guard with `recorder`
  unset, so an aborted tail still closes the watchers. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **Row before ending.** *Fork:* close the watchers in the drop at once and record afterwards, or
  close them only once the row is written. *Ruling:* the latter: when the guard spawns the tail,
  `end_run` closes the watchers after `settle`, as on the ordinary path. *Reasoning:* closed
  first, a caller that reads `status_for` the moment it hears the ending can still read the run
  as open, and a trigger in that window starts a second run beside an open row. Closed after, a
  trigger in the window joins the dying run and is told its ending. The cost is that the ending
  now waits for `settle`'s statements, bounded by the pool's own timeouts. *Reversing:* low.
- **The backoff.** *Fork:* treat the panic as the cancelled run is treated (no verdict, no
  backoff), or as an `error`. *Ruling:* an `error`: one rung up the ladder, no credential verdict,
  a stored `unreachable` cleared, as for a protocol bug. *Reasoning:* a panic is the adapter's
  fault, not the reader's, and an adapter that panics every run should back off like one that
  errors every run. `reconcile_abandoned` writes `error` too, so the ladder already counted these
  rows after a restart. *Reversing:* one constructor.
- **The message.** *Fork:* keep `RUN_STOPPED_MESSAGE`'s text or change it. *Ruling:* it now reads
  "the run stopped before it could finish". *Reasoning:* the old "without recording an outcome"
  became false once the guard records one, and the row now stores the text. Nothing outside
  `scheduler.rs` matched the old text. *Reversing:* one string.
- **A §10.8 entry.** *Ruling:* booked (`1638-a-panicked-run-is-recorded.md`). `knobas-sync` is not
  frozen, but `sync:state`, `sync_status` and `list_sources` observably change for a panicked run,
  as they did for #1629's cancelled run. *Reversing:* n/a.

### #1638: merge-manager review (Opus, 2026-10-23)

- **A drop on a runtime that is shutting down.** *Fork:* guard the spawn further, or rely on
  `Handle::try_current` plus tokio's handling of a spawn onto a closed runtime. *Ruling:* as
  written. *Reasoning:* off a runtime the guard falls through to closing the watchers; on one that
  is shutting down, tokio 1.53 shuts the new task down at bind instead of panicking, and dropping
  its future runs the inner guard (`recorder` unset), which closes the watchers. Neither path can
  panic during the unwind or re-enter `Background`'s lock. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **The quit racing the spawn.** *Ruling:* no gap. `Background::spawn` checks the closed state and
  spawns under one lock, and `close` takes the set under the same lock, so a tail either lands in
  the set the quit awaits or is refused. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **Panic versus cancel for the ladder.** *Ruling:* the distinction is drawn by the right signal.
  `was_cancelled` and `failures_since_last_ok` key on `CANCELLED_MESSAGE`, which only
  `RunResult::cancelled` writes; the guard writes `RUN_STOPPED_MESSAGE`, so #1629's cancelled run
  still does not back off and a panic does. *Reversing:* one constructor.
- **§10.8 wording.** *Ruling:* the entry now also says a panic after the quit has begun keeps the
  old treatment (watchers closed, row left to `reconcile_abandoned`), since that is observable and
  the entry named only the abort. *Reversing:* one sentence.

## #1802: two load flakes, a limiter bound and an ownership lock (Opus implementer, 2026-10-23)

- **The adoption failure is not a race in `start_managed`'s claim.** *Fork:* fix the claim, or
  fix how the lock is released. *Ruling:* the release. *Reasoning:* the refusal named the test
  binary's own pid, which only this test's processes could have written into its tempdir's
  `.owner.lock`. A child another test thread was spawning held a copy of the dropped descriptor
  between its fork and its exec, and an flock lasts until the last copy closes. Reproduced alone in
  a 40-line program (296 of 2,000 reclaims refused beside four spawning threads, 0 without them, 0
  with an explicit unlock) and in the new unit test (106 of 300). `OwnerLock` unlocks on drop.
  *Reversing:* low, the newtype is the only change.
- **No §10.8 entry.** *Fork:* book the unlock as an observable change, or not. *Ruling:* none owed. *Reasoning:* no IPC, migration or module-layout change;
  a shipped process releases the lock only as it quits, and `restart` keeps it. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **Cross-run collision ruled out for the adoption test.** *Fork:* a shared port, data directory or temp path between
  test binaries or worktrees, or a cause inside one binary. *Ruling:* inside one binary.
  *Reasoning:* every embedded test takes its own
  `tempfile::tempdir()` (data directory, both lock files), and a fresh start asks for port 0. A
  shared port fails a start with a bind error, never with *has this profile open*.
  *Reversing:* n/a.
- **The bring-up lock keeps closing without an unlock.** *Fork:* give it the same unlock-on-drop, or
  leave it. *Ruling:* unchanged. *Reasoning:* a
  bring-up waits for its lock (50 ms polls), so a child's copy delays it by one exec and refuses
  nothing. *Reversing:* low.
- **The two sibling limiter tests with a literal refill bound get the measured one too.** *Fork:*
  the named test only, or every test bounded by "what refills while the test runs". *Ruling:* all
  three (`a_loosening_right_away_takes_nothing_from_a_full_limiter`, `a_request_ends_the_quiet`,
  `a_request_ends_the_quiet_before_a_loosening`). *Reasoning:* same assertion shape, same cause;
  the others' literals had 100 to 300 ms of margin where the named one had 10. The tests asserting a
  floor or a whole burst are left alone: a stall only adds refill up to the burst.
  *Reversing:* low.
- **The bound adds one request to what the elapsed time refilled.** *Fork:* the bare elapsed
  refill, or one more. *Ruling:* one more. *Reasoning:* governor reads
  `quanta`'s clock and the test reads `Instant`, and the two can round a refill differently; the
  one is the original test's own allowance at a zero-length window, not a wider tolerance.
  *Reversing:* low.
- **#1808 (a silent port another bind can take) is fixed here; #1809 is left.** *Fork:* the
  orchestrator asked for both if they share a cause. *Ruling:* #1808 shares the class (how the
  embedded tests pick ports) and failed once in this ticket's own 22 runs, so `SilentPort` holds a
  bound, never-listened socket for each of the three tests that dropped one. #1809 is a scheduler
  gap bound in `knobas-app`'s bring-up test; its fix needs a marker inside the migration step,
  which is neither of the causes here. *Reversing:* low.
- **A cross-binary collision does exist, in one test, and the test takes the reaper's lock.**
  *Fork:* leave `on_a_server_of_its_own_each_source_file_gets_a_database_of_its_own` to the
  reaper's rules, or hold the child's scratch lock while adopting its orphan. *Ruling:* hold it.
  *Reasoning:* two `embedded` binaries side by side went red 2 times in 9 with *pg_ctl: directory
  ... is not a database cluster directory*: the child's `$TMPDIR/knobas-test-<pid>` is abandoned
  by design once it exits, so the other binary's reaper (and any gate's `knobas-test-server`)
  stopped and deleted it between this test's adoption and its stop. Locking the sibling
  `knobas-test-<pid>.lock` first, blocking, is what a reaper itself does, so every reaper passes the
  root by; a reaper that got there first leaves no `postmaster.pid` and the adoption is skipped.
  Test-only; the reaper and the product are unchanged. *Reversing:* low.
- **Merge-manager deep pass: unlock-on-drop is the fix, not close-on-exec (Opus merge-manager,
  2026-10-23).** *Fork:* open `.owner.lock` close-on-exec as the root fix, or keep the unlock.
  *Ruling:* keep the unlock; nothing to add. *Reasoning:* the descriptor is already close-on-exec:
  `std::fs::OpenOptions` opens every file with `O_CLOEXEC`, so no exec'd child (the postmaster
  included, which `pg_ctl` execs) keeps a copy past its exec. The window is fork to exec, which
  close-on-exec cannot close and an unlock does. `File::try_lock`/`unlock` are `flock(2)` on Unix,
  so the lock belongs to the open file description: `LOCK_UN` releases it for every copy of that
  descriptor, and for no other. `claim_ownership` opens a new description on each call and the
  file is never `try_clone`d, so a second claim in the same process is refused rather than
  sharing the lock, and dropping one `OwnerLock` cannot release a lock another handle still
  needs. `EmbeddedDb` declares `owner_lock` last, so the unlock still follows the server's stop.
  *Reversing:* low.
## #1640: a body cap, no redirected write, no userinfo in a base URL (Opus implementer, 2026-10-23)

- **Reserved for Björn, ruled by implementer on Opus (waiver of 2026-10-22): the frozen-surface
  change to `crates/knobas-http/**` and `crates/knobas-source/src/**`.** *Fork:* change both, or
  leave #1640 open until Björn signs it off. *Ruling:* change them, booked in
  `docs/contract/10.8/1640-knobas-http-body-cap-no-redirected-write-no-userinfo.md`. The limiter
  and #1729's `watch_local_quota` mark are untouched. *Reasoning:* spec #1620 ruling C2 names
  these changes and the waiver covers its frozen-surface steps. `HttpConfig::max_body` is a new
  public field, so the six adapter struct literals that name every field gain one line.
  *Reversing:* medium: the field, the module, the second client.
- **Which reads the cap covers.** *Fork:* this crate's own reads (`get_json`, `get_json_with`,
  the error body), or every body `send` hands back. *Ruling:* every body `send` hands back for a
  success, re-wrapped through `http::Response` and read through a counting `http_body::Body`. A
  `send_streaming` body is exempt. *Reasoning:* Confluence's listings, Gitea's JSON reads and the
  Jira writes call `response.json()` themselves, and a cap that skipped them would leave the
  review's scenario open. A download is large on purpose and has its stall bound (#1012).
  *Cost:* none left: the re-wrap keeps the response's URL (merge-manager's fix, below).
  *Reversing:* low.
- **Where the declared length is checked.** *Fork:* in the counting body (every reader), or in
  the reads that take the body whole. *Ruling:* in the whole-body reads (`cap::declared_over`).
  *Reasoning:* Gitea's `raw_capped` (#711) reads the first megabyte of a file of any size and
  stops. A body that refused a long declared length up front would turn its cut view of a 40 MiB
  file into an error. *Reversing:* low.
- **An error body over the cap.** *Fork:* fail it as `Protocol { status: None }` naming the cap,
  or keep the status's class and put the cap's sentence where the excerpt goes. *Ruling:* keep
  the class. *Reasoning:* a 503 with a huge body must still be retried and a 401 must still ask
  for the credential. A 4xx is still `Protocol` naming the cap, which is the ticket's wording.
  *Reversing:* low.
- **A write whose success answer is over the cap.** *Ruling:* the wrap is lazy, so the write is
  sent and answered, and only the adapter's read of the answer fails, the same as an undecodable
  answer today. *Reasoning:* failing inside `send` would record as refused a write that happened.
  *Reversing:* n/a.
- **How a write is kept off redirects.** *Fork:* a custom redirect policy, or a second client.
  *Ruling:* a second reqwest client with `Policy::none()` for every method but `GET`/`HEAD`.
  *Reasoning:* reqwest 0.13's `redirect::Attempt` carries the status and URLs but not the method,
  so no policy can tell a POST from a GET. *Cost:* a second connection pool and TLS config per
  `HttpClient`. *Reversing:* low.
- **Which redirects a write refuses.** *Ruling:* every 3xx, 307 and 308 included, and 303 too.
  *Reasoning:* the ticket says never follow one. A 307 re-send to an address knobas was not
  configured with is still a guess about the proxy (C2). A 303 after a POST (post/redirect/get)
  can mean the write happened, but no write endpoint knobas uses answers that way, and the
  refusal names the target either way. *Reversing:* one match arm.
- **The redirected write's status.** *Fork:* `Protocol { status: None }` as the dispatch
  expected, or the 3xx. *Ruling:* `Some(<3xx>)`. *Reasoning:* `SourceError::Protocol`'s doc says
  `status` is set when the failure came from a response. The write queue's `retryable` reads any
  status under 500 other than 408 and 429 as a refusal, so the write is recorded refused with the
  `Location` in its reason either way (a row in its table test says so). The quota mark (#1729)
  never applies, since the source answered. *Reversing:* one field.
- **The `Location` as given.** *Ruling:* printed raw, not resolved against the request URL.
  *Reasoning:* it is what the proxy said, and a test can match it exactly. *Reversing:* low.
- **What counts as userinfo, and where it is refused.** *Ruling:* a username alone too
  (`username()` non-empty or `password()` set, as the wasm guard reads it), refused in `http_url`
  so `InstanceLimiter::for_url` refuses it too, and at `crud::add` and `crud::update` through
  `knobas_http::refuse_userinfo`, before the keychain is written. The draft *Test* path gets no
  check of its own: every adapter that reaches the network builds an `HttpClient`, which refuses.
  *Reasoning:* `check_id`'s rule: the form uses the client's function, not a copy. *Reversing:*
  low.
- **The redaction helper.** *Fork:* a private mask in each crate, or one public function.
  *Ruling:* `knobas_source::instance::redact_userinfo`, by string, used by `SourceInstance`'s and
  `HttpConfig`'s `Debug` and by `http_url`'s parse-failure message. *Reasoning:* it has to mask a
  URL that does not parse, so `url` cannot do it. `knobas-http` already depends on
  `knobas-source`, so one function serves both. It is blunt (everything before the authority's
  last `@`, a `/` included) because a false positive costs a masked host in a log line.
  *Reversing:* low.
- **`remote.rs`'s cap.** *Ruling:* folded in, as spec #1620 allowed: the adapter fetch builds its
  client with its own cap as `max_body`, and maps `over_the_cap` to `TooLarge`. Its
  read-then-measure check is removed. *Reasoning:* a component may be up to 64 MiB, over the
  default, so the default would have broken an install between 32 and 64 MiB. *Reversing:* low.
- **The cap's value.** *Ruling:* 32 MiB. *Reasoning:* "tens of MiB": far over a hundred-issue
  Jira page, far under what the app can hold beside Postgres. *Reversing:* one constant.
- **The dialog showing the reason.** *Ruling:* witnessed by the crud test's IPC mapping (`to_ipc`
  gives `invalid` and the message) plus the existing #1506 vitest, which shows a rejected save's
  `ipcErrorMessage` in the dialog's alert. No new vitest. *Reasoning:* the dialog does not branch
  on this reason, so a test with this message would repeat #1506's. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **A live run.** *Ruling:* none owed. *Reasoning:* the redirect change acts only when a source
  answers a write with a 3xx. A live write suite that passes today checks that its write landed,
  which a write turned into a GET would not, so none passes through a redirect now. The
  second client differs from the first only in its redirect policy, and the local transport
  tests send JSON and text bodies through it. The cap is far over any seeded page, a TeamCity
  log goes through `send_streaming`, and Gitea's file read stops at its own cap (tested
  locally). *Reversing:* n/a.

## #1637 and #1642: a half-written data directory, `initdb`'s kill, and a private password file (Opus implementer, 2026-10-23)

- **Reproduce first (#1637).** *Fork:* reproduce "postgresql.conf without PG_VERSION fails every
  launch", or refute it. *Ruling:* reproduced, and that shape is rare. *Reasoning:* the launch on
  such a directory failed with *not a database cluster directory* (the red
  `a_data_directory_an_interrupted_initdb_left_is_initialised_again`). How it arises, from
  PostgreSQL 18.6 on this Mac (scripts `issue-1637-e*.py` in that run's scratchpad):
  1. `initdb` writes `PG_VERSION` before `postgresql.conf`. 55 runs froze `initdb` and its
     children with `SIGSTOP` 20 to 450 ms in (a full `initdb` takes about 0.4 s), copied the
     directory, then killed them. Every copy had both files. That is the shape a power loss
     leaves. None of the copies had `postgresql.conf` without `PG_VERSION`.
  2. The shape arose once, in about 340 kills: `initdb` was failing on its own and was killed
     during its cleanup. The cleanup's `rmtree` removes `PG_VERSION` before `postgresql.conf`.
  3. On the copies, a start fails with *could not find the database system* (no `pg_control`,
     up to ~50 ms in), or starts a server that refuses our password (before `setup_auth`), or one
     that lacks the `postgres` database. Each fails every launch, as the ticket says, and is
     filed as #1819.
  *Reversing:* n/a.
- **What may be removed.** *Fork:* the shape the ticket names, or any directory that fails to
  start. *Ruling:* only `postgresql.conf` present and `PG_VERSION` absent, as
  the dispatch requires, checked with `symlink_metadata`. An entry that cannot be examined counts
  as present, so a `PG_VERSION` that cannot be `stat`ed keeps the directory. It runs in
  `start_managed` after the ownership claim and the password read, under both locks, before
  setup. *Reasoning:* a directory without `PG_VERSION` was never a cluster, and PostgreSQL will
  not start on it, so no server is running there either. `Path::exists` reads a permission
  error as "absent" and would have deleted a real cluster over a bad mode. *Reversing:* one
  predicate.
- **The PG_VERSION shapes are not recovered here.** *Fork:* widen the removal to them here, or
  file them. *Ruling:* filed as #1819
  (`ready-for-agent`, Opus). It asks for a ruling on a marker that tells a finished `initdb`
  from a killed one. *Reasoning:* the dispatch forbids removing a directory with `PG_VERSION`.
  Without a marker, no on-disk test separates a killed `initdb` from a reader's database with a
  missing file. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **How `initdb` gets `kill_on_drop`.** *Fork:* patch around the crate, or run `initdb`
  ourselves. *Ruling:* knobas runs it (`initialise` and `run_initdb`), with the crate's flags.
  `setup()` then finds `postgresql.conf` and skips its own. *Reasoning:* `postgresql_embedded`
  0.21 builds the `tokio::process::Command` inside its private `initialize()`, so nothing can
  set `kill_on_drop` there. *Reversing:* medium. Delete the two functions and `setup()` runs
  `initdb` again.
- **Installing without `initdb`.** *Fork:* call `postgresql_archive`'s `get_archive` and
  `extract` directly, or let the crate's `setup()` install. *Ruling:* `setup()` installs, pointed
  at a placeholder data directory (`<root>/.install-only`) that holds an empty `postgresql.conf`,
  which `setup()` takes for initialised. The placeholder is removed afterwards. *Reasoning:* a
  cold machine then downloads and unpacks through the crate's own code, and `PostgreSQL::new`
  resolves the version directory. A copy of the install path would drift from the crate, and no
  local test runs a cold install. *Reversing:* low.
- **A timeout sends `SIGTERM` before the kill.** *Fork:* `kill_on_drop` alone, or `SIGTERM`,
  a 10 s grace, then the drop's `SIGKILL`. *Ruling:* `SIGTERM` first. *Reasoning:* 40 `SIGTERM`s
  10 to 400 ms in all left no data directory, because `initdb` traps the signal and removes what
  it made. A `SIGKILL` leaves the `PG_VERSION` shape of #1819, which fails every launch. Without
  the kill, the old crate path let `initdb` run on. A drop, which cannot wait, still kills. Both
  are tested: `a_timed_out_initdb_is_stopped_and_removes_what_it_made` and
  `a_dropped_initdb_is_killed_with_its_future`. *Reversing:* low.
- **The password file's mode (#1642).** *Fork:* chmod after setup only, or also create the file
  0600. *Ruling:* created 0600 (`OpenOptionsExt::mode`) when
  knobas writes it, and set to 0600 after every `setup()`, so a 0644 file an older build left is
  tightened too. The data directory is set to 0700 when it is wider (PostgreSQL also accepts
  0750). Both only on `cfg(unix)`. *Reasoning:* the ticket asks for 0600 after setup. Writing it
  0600 also closes the moment between creation and the chmod. *Reversing:* low.
- **A failed chmod is logged, not returned.** *Fork:* fail the launch, or warn. *Ruling:* warn.
  *Reasoning:* knobas owns the file, so a chmod can fail only on a volume that does not keep
  Unix modes. Failing there would fail every launch over a mode the volume cannot hold.
  *Reversing:* one match arm.
- **§10.8.** *Fork:* book the recovery as a boot-screen change, or not. *Ruling:* none owed. *Reasoning:* no IPC type, migration or module-layout change.
  No boot-screen state or message changes. A directory that used to fail now starts, and an
  `initdb` failure reads as before (`DatabaseInitializationError` with the command's output, or
  *deadline has elapsed*). *Reversing:* n/a.
- **SysV segments left by the experiments.** *Fork:* leave the segments for the reaper, or
  remove them by hand. *Ruling:* removed by hand. *Reasoning:* killing `initdb`'s whole process
  group with `SIGKILL` during the first experiment left 31 SysV segments from its bootstrap
  backends. With `kern.sysv.shmmni` at 32, every new PostgreSQL on the machine failed with *could
  not create shared memory segment* from about 07:08 to 07:13. PostgreSQL reclaims a stale
  segment only when the same data directory starts again, and those directories were gone. The
  31 were removed by their creator pids (the experiment's dead `postgres` children, `NATTCH` 0).
  Later experiments removed the segments their own processes created. A run that kills only `initdb`, as `kill_on_drop` does, leaves none: the
  backend reads EOF and exits. *Reversing:* n/a.

### #1637 and #1642: merge-manager review (Opus, 2026-10-23)

- **A symlinked data directory.** *Fork:* resolve the link and remove what it points at, or
  remove the link alone. *Ruling:* the link alone, which `std::fs::remove_dir_all` already does:
  it follows no symlink, so the target keeps every file and `initdb` makes a real `data/` in the
  link's place. *Reasoning:* a wrong removal loses a database; a removed link loses nothing.
  Witnessed by `a_half_written_symlinked_data_directory_loses_the_link_alone` (a mutant that
  removes the canonical path dies). *Reversing:* low.
- **"Under both locks" holds on every path.** *Fork:* guard `remove_half_written` itself, or rely
  on its one caller. *Ruling:* rely on it. *Reasoning:* `start_managed` is its only caller, and
  every bring-up reaches it through `launch`: the first launch, the stale-lock retry, and #1779's
  restart after *Failed* (`EmbeddedDb::start` again). A restore is a logical `pg_restore` over
  the connector and never touches `data/`. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **The install placeholder leaves nothing behind.** *Fork:* accept the placeholder, or install
  through `postgresql_archive`. *Ruling:* accept it. *Reasoning:* in `postgresql_embedded` 0.21
  `setup()` writes the password file only inside `initialize()`, which the placeholder's empty
  `postgresql.conf` skips. The handle's drop stops nothing (no `postmaster.pid`) and deletes
  nothing (`temporary` is false). A placeholder a kill left is rewritten and removed by the next
  launch. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **`initdb` matches the crate's.** *Fork:* accept the copy as is, or align it. *Ruling:* aligned
  on the one difference. The arguments are the crate's, in its order (`--auth password --pgdata
  --encoding UTF8 --pwfile --username postgres`), with no environment and stdin closed, as
  `output()` leaves it, under the same 60 s limit. The crate also sets `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` on
  Windows. knobas now sets it too, under `cfg(windows)`, which this Mac does not compile.
  *Reasoning:* a data directory either `initdb` made is the same. A profile that is already
  initialised skips `initialise` before the install, so it starts as before; only the two modes
  change. *Reversing:* one line.
## #1818: a read the server hung up on is sent again (Opus implementer, 2026-10-23)

- **Reserved for Björn, ruled by implementer on Opus (waiver of 2026-10-22): the frozen-surface
  change** to `crates/knobas-http/**`. *Fork:* change the frozen crate, or leave #1818 open for
  Björn. *Ruling:* make it, booked in
  `docs/contract/10.8/1818-knobas-http-a-read-the-server-hung-up-on-is-sent-again.md`: one new
  public predicate, `retry::closed_before_answering`, one dependency (`hyper`, already in the
  tree through reqwest), and one more transient case in `send_with`. *Reasoning:* the ticket
  names the change and the model; the limiter (#1630, #1728, #1740, #1764, #1771), the quota mark
  (#1729) and #1640's cap and second client are untouched. *Reversing:* low, one branch.
- **Retry the read, or shorten the pool's idle timeout.** *Fork:* the ticket's two options.
  *Ruling:* send a `GET` or `HEAD` once more when hyper reports `IncompleteMessage` from `send`.
  *Reasoning:* the race is between the client's reuse and *any* server's idle timeout, and a
  `pool_idle_timeout` only wins it against servers whose timeout is above the number picked:
  Node's 5 s, Apache's 5 s and gunicorn's 2 s sit at or below anything that still pools usefully,
  so the number would be a guess about every source a person might add. A retry covers every
  server, costs nothing until the race happens, and goes through the attempt loop, so it passes
  the limiter and fits the send budget as every retry does. *Reversing:* low.
- **"On a reused connection".** *Fork:* resend only when the connection was a pooled one, or on
  any `IncompleteMessage`. *Ruling:* any, once per call. *Reasoning:* hyper-util knows whether a
  connection was reused but reqwest's error does not say; for a safe method the distinction does
  not change what a resend can do, and "once" is the bound that keeps a server that hangs up on
  every request from costing `MAX_ATTEMPTS`. *Reversing:* low.
- **Writes.** *Fork:* let a write that did not opt out retry too. *Ruling:* no; any method other
  than `GET` or `HEAD`, and any request with `no_retry`, is not sent again and keeps its
  `Protocol { status: None }` reading. *Reasoning:* the server read the request whole before it
  closed; whether it acted is unknown, and ADR-0012's once-sent reading is the ticket's
  constraint. Whether that reading should be `Unconfirmed` rather than `Protocol` is outside the
  ticket: #1821. *Reversing:* low.
- **A reset rather than a close.** *Fork:* also resend a read whose connection was reset
  (`ECONNRESET`) before answering. *Ruling:* no, `IncompleteMessage` only, as the ticket names.
  *Reasoning:* the seen failure is the clean close; the reset shape has not been seen here and
  would widen the retry past the diagnosis. *Reversing:* low.

### #1818 merge review (Opus merge-manager, 2026-10-23)

- **Reserved for Björn, the frozen-surface change: the implementer's ruling stands.** *Fork:*
  confirm the change to `crates/knobas-http/**`, or hold it for Björn. *Ruling:* confirmed. The
  resend sits in `send_with`'s transport classifier, behind `retry` and `follows`, so the
  limiter, the budget check, the quota mark, #1640's cap and second client and every
  `SourceError` mapping are as on main; the §10.8 entry matches the diff. `hyper = "1"` resolves
  to the one `hyper` 1.11.0 already in `Cargo.lock`, and the gate has no dependency allowlist.
  *Reasoning:* a two-close `GET` ends on its second attempt with the second attempt's
  `Protocol { status: None }`, never loops, and a write never takes this path. *Reversing:*
  low.
- **Does `no_retry` stop the resend of a `GET`?** *Fork:* resend any `GET` or `HEAD`, or none
  that opted out. *Ruling:* none that opted out, as the code already does (`no_retry` takes the
  once-sent branch). *Reasoning:* `Request::no_retry`'s doc promises one sending; a read that asked
  for it is rare (no adapter does) but gets what it asked for. Pinned by the new
  `hung_up::a_read_sent_with_no_retry_is_not_sent_again`, which fails if the once-sent branch
  also resends a read. *Reversing:* low.

## #1821: a write the server hung up on before answering (Opus implementer, 2026-10-23)

- **Reserved for Björn, ruled by implementer on Opus (waiver of 2026-10-22): the frozen-surface
  change** to `crates/knobas-http/**`. *Fork:* change the frozen crate, or leave the reading as
  it is. *Ruling:* change it, booked in
  `docs/contract/10.8/1821-knobas-http-a-write-the-server-hung-up-on-is-unconfirmed.md`: one
  new branch in `send_with`'s transport classifier and one new public constant. *Reasoning:* the
  ticket names the change and the waiver lets an Opus implementer rule it; the limiter, the quota
  mark, #1640's changes and #1818's resend of a read are untouched. *Reversing:* low.
- **The reading (fork a).** *Fork:* keep `Protocol { status: None }` (refused by the queue), or
  read the hang-up as `Unconfirmed { status: None }` through `classify::once_sent`. *Ruling:*
  `Unconfirmed`. *Reasoning:* the server read the request whole and gave no answer, which is
  ADR-0012's (#1125's) case of a request that reached the source and got none, the same as a
  timeout or a `502`/`504`. Refused was the one wrong reading: a ticket that may stand at the
  source showed as one that never would. The queue now holds a write a second arrival would
  duplicate and ladders one whose resend is harmless, as #1627 does for Kuma. *Reversing:* low.
- **Which requests read so.** *Fork:* `no_retry` writes only, every write, or every request not
  sent again for the hang-up. *Ruling:* every request not sent again for it: any method but `GET`
  and `HEAD`, retries or not, and any request sent with `no_retry`, a `GET` included. A `GET` or
  `HEAD` with retries is sent once more (#1818), and its second hang-up stays `Protocol`.
  *Reasoning:* a write that kept retries was still sent once on this failure (#1818 never resends
  one), so it is in the same doubt; the #1122 audit gave retries to writes whose resend is
  harmless, so the queue ladders them. A `no_retry` read is `once_sent`'s domain like any
  once-sent request, and `Unconfirmed` reads as `Unreachable` everywhere outside the write queue.
  This supersedes #1818's "Writes" ruling, which left this to #1821. *Reversing:* low.
- **How it goes through `once_sent`.** *Fork:* a new public classifier, a new parameter on
  `once_sent`, or hand the hang-up in as what it is to `once_sent`. *Ruling:* the last:
  `once_sent(Unreachable(<message>), connected = true)`. *Reasoning:* the server did not answer,
  which is `Unreachable`'s meaning, and the connection had opened; `once_sent` already maps that
  to `Unconfirmed`, so the frozen signature stays and no second rule exists. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **A `pool_idle_timeout` on the write client (fork b).** *Fork:* none, one on both clients, one
  on the write client, or no pooling for writes at all. *Ruling:* 4 s on the write client only
  (`WRITE_POOL_IDLE`). *Reasoning:* reads are covered by #1818's resend, so #1818's ruling
  against a timeout stands for them. A write has no resend, and under fork a the race now costs
  the reader a held create to check. Kuma's socket.io packets go on the write client and Node's
  keep-alive is 5 s (Apache's too) against Kuma's 15 s `IDLE_REUSE`, so a held session's emit
  could meet the close; 4 s lets the connection go first, and the cost is one fresh connection
  for a write after a pause. No pooling at all would cost a handshake per packet of every Kuma
  exchange. A server with a shorter keep-alive (gunicorn's 2 s) can still race, and fork a reads
  that honestly. *Reversing:* trivial (one builder call).
- **Kuma's poll path.** *Fork:* change the Kuma adapter too, or not. *Ruling:* no adapter change.
  *Reasoning:* the GET polls stay on the read client, and engine.io's polling session is named
  by its `sid`, not bound to a connection, so a packet on a fresh connection is the same packet.
  A hang-up on the write's emit is now `Unconfirmed`, which `call_with` returns as it does a lost
  ack (#1627); one on a login packet is `Unconfirmed` turned `Unreachable` by `not_yet_emitted`,
  so the write waits on the ladder where it was refused before. `just kuma-live` ran once to
  witness the write client's change. *Reversing:* low.

- **Reserved for Björn, ruled by implementer on Opus: the frozen-surface change.** *Fork:* uphold

- **The idle-timeout test sleeps a real 4.5 s.** *Fork:* accept, or make `WRITE_POOL_IDLE`

- **`just kuma-live` on `3b739a9b`, not the head.** *Fork:* re-run on the head or accept.

## #1819: a data directory a killed `initdb` left with `PG_VERSION` in it (Opus implementer, 2026-10-23)

- **Reserved for Björn, ruled by implementer on Opus (waiver of 2026-10-22): reversing #1637's
  "never with `PG_VERSION`".** *Fork:* keep the rule, or reverse it for the shapes a killed
  `initdb` leaves. *Ruling:* reversed for a data directory that has no knobas marker and holds no
  database. Any other directory with `PG_VERSION` is still never removed. *Reasoning:* spec #1619
  reserves this step, and the waiver lets an Opus agent rule it. A killed `initdb` fails every
  launch until the reader deletes `data/` by hand, and the rule below never matches a directory
  a finished `initdb` made. *Reversing:* one predicate (`shape`).
- **What marks a directory deletable.** *Fork:* the ticket's marker with its example migration
  rule (`PG_VERSION`, `global/pg_control` and `base/5` get the marker), an `initdb` into a temp
  sibling renamed into place, or an on-disk test alone. *Ruling:* a marker
  (`knobas-initdb-finished` in the data directory), written after knobas's `initdb` returns
  success, plus a test for directories without one. A directory without the marker is removed
  only when it **holds no database**: nothing under `base/` but the templates `1` and `4`, and
  nothing under `pg_tblspc/`. Every other unmarked directory with `PG_VERSION` is marked the
  first time a launch sees it, and is never removed after that. *Reasoning:* `initdb` makes
  `base/5`, the `postgres` database, last. The reader's data lives in the `knobas` database,
  which a launch creates after that. So a finished `initdb` from any build always leaves a
  directory that is not `1` or `4`. Every build has run 18.6, and on PostgreSQL before 15, where
  `postgres` and `template0` had no fixed OIDs, a finished cluster still has one. The ticket's
  example reads in the other direction: a directory it would not mark (no `base/5`, but a
  `knobas` database) would then be judged by its absence. Here the migration rule is the exact
  complement of the removal test, so no directory falls between the two. A doubt about a database
  keeps the directory: a marker that cannot be `stat`ed counts as present, and a `base/` or
  `pg_tblspc/` that cannot be listed counts as holding a database. The marker matters after the first sight:
  once a directory is marked, nothing it loses later (a dropped `postgres`, a damaged `base/`)
  can make a launch remove it. *Reversing:* low. Without the marker, the test runs on every
  launch.
- **No temp sibling and rename.** *Fork:* `initdb` into `data.partial` and rename it to `data`
  on success, so a half-made directory never has the final name, or the marker. *Ruling:* the
  marker. *Reasoning:* the rename does not remove the test. Directories that older builds' killed
  `initdb`s left are already named `data`, and the ticket asks for them back. Without a marker,
  a renamed directory cannot be told from an older build's either, so the test would run on
  every launch. The rename also replaces a symlinked `data/`, which #1637's review ruled
  supported, and it fails across volumes when the link points at another volume. *Reversing:*
  medium.
- **An unfinished directory a server answers for is kept.** *Fork:* remove it under a running
  postmaster, or keep it. *Ruling:* kept when `postmaster.pid` names a postmaster (a positive
  pid) and something answers on its port, or when the file cannot be read. *Reasoning:* a server
  on such a directory is one an older build started and lost, and its files are not deleted
  under it. `initdb`'s own backends run standalone and write a lock that records their pid
  negated and the default port 5432 (read during a real `initdb`). Without the sign check, a lock
  a power loss left would keep the directory whenever any PostgreSQL answers on 5432.
  *Reversing:* one function (`served`).
- **No check for a concurrent `initdb`.** *Fork:* check for a live writer before removing, or
  rely on the locks. *Ruling:* the locks. *Reasoning:* the removal runs under `bring_up_lock` and
  the ownership lock, and every build since M0 (#12, 2026-08-24) has taken `bring_up_lock`
  before `initdb`. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **The three states, made by a real kill.** *Fork:* fixtures written by hand, a `SIGSTOP` copy
  as #1637's evidence used, or the production kill. *Ruling:* the production kill:
  `run_initdb`'s future is dropped (`kill_on_drop`, `SIGKILL` to `initdb` alone) at a point read
  from the directory and the process tree, and the children then drain what `initdb` piped them
  and exit. *Reasoning:* that is the directory a given-up bring-up leaves. Each state was named by
  starting a server on what the kill left and logging in with our password (16 runs, scripts
  `issue-1819-*.py` in that run's scratchpad, PostgreSQL 18.6 on this Mac):
  1. Killed when `postgresql.conf` appears (the `--check` probes): *could not find the database
     system*, 4 of 4.
  2. Killed when `global/pg_control` is there and the `--boot` child runs: *password
     authentication failed*, 4 of 4.
  3. Killed when the `--single` child appears: *database "postgres" does not exist*, 8 of 8.
     About 25 ms later `initdb` has piped every command, and a kill then leaves a finished
     directory (base `1`, `4`, `5` at 30, 40, 40 and 100 ms).
  In each, base holds `1` alone. `each_directory_a_killed_initdb_leaves_comes_back_from_a_launch`
  makes the three states and launches on each. It failed on the pre-#1819 code (state 1:
  *Connection reset by peer* after 60 s). No run of it, and no late kill with `initdb`'s pipes
  closed, left a shared-memory segment. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **An older build's directory, witnessed.** *Fork:* prove the migration in tests alone, or on a
  directory main made. *Ruling:* both. *Reasoning:* main at 2c219532 (`EmbeddedDb::start`)
  initialised a profile and wrote a row. Two launches of this build then read the row back, and
  the first wrote the marker. In the tree,
  `a_directory_a_finished_initdb_made_is_never_removed` runs #1637's `initdb` to the end with no
  start, and the crate's own `setup()` with a `knobas` database and a row (every build before
  #1637). Each is kept and marked. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **#1637's never-removed test.** *Fork:* keep it, or replace it. *Ruling:* replaced by
  `a_data_directory_that_holds_a_database_is_never_removed`. *Reasoning:* its fixtures (empty
  `base/`, `PG_VERSION`) are what this ruling now removes. The new one gives each fixture a
  database (`base/16384`, `base/5`, `pg_tblspc/16385`) and no `pg_control`, so only the database
  keeps it. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **Test seams.** *Fork:* confirm the seams with Björn first, as the TDD skill asks, or pick them.
  *Ruling:* picked, since the loop runs unattended. `EmbeddedDb::start` for what a launch does,
  and `recover_or_mark` and `shape` in the crate for the doubt paths no launch can set up.
  *Reversing:* n/a.
- **§10.8.** *Fork:* book the recovery as a boot-screen change, or not. *Ruling:* none owed.
  *Reasoning:* no IPC type, migration, module layout, boot-screen state or message changes. A
  directory that failed every launch now starts, and only the log line's text is new.
  *Reversing:* n/a.
- **SysV segments and a stray server.** *Fork:* free what appeared during the run, or only what
  is provably ours. *Ruling:* only ours. *Reasoning:* the first red run left a server (pid 15283)
  from a test that panicked while it held one. It exited on its own within a minute, once its
  temp directory was gone, and the tests now stop their server before they assert. A segment
  whose creator, pid 24266, was dead (`NATTCH` 0, 08:00:01) appeared during another run. No
  rerun of mine reproduced it, and sibling runs were starting servers too, so it was left.
  *Reversing:* n/a.

## #1819 / PR #1824: merge-manager review (Opus merge-manager, 2026-10-23)

- **A missing `base/` or `pg_tblspc/` keeps the directory.** *Fork:* read a `base/` or
  `pg_tblspc/` that is not found as empty, as the PR did, or as a doubt. *Ruling:* a doubt, so
  the directory counts as holding a database. *Reasoning:* `initdb` makes both before it writes
  `PG_VERSION`, so no killed `initdb` lacks either. What does lack one is a `base/` symlinked to a
  volume that is not mounted: `read_dir` reports *not found*, the directory read as unfinished,
  and `remove_dir_all` took `global/`, `pg_wal/` and the rest with it, leaving the reader's
  databases on that volume with no cluster to open them. Red before the fix:
  `a_directory_whose_databases_are_on_a_missing_volume_is_kept` (`base`). The fixtures of the
  unfinished-directory tests and of `a_data_directory_that_holds_a_database_is_never_removed` now
  have the empty `pg_tblspc/` every killed `initdb` has, so each is still decided by its database
  (mutant M2 rerun: it dies). *Reversing:* one match arm.
- **The predicate, checked on 18.6.** A complete `initdb` with this machine's 18.6 binaries
  leaves `base/` holding `1`, `4` and `5`, and `pg_tblspc/` empty, so no finished directory reads
  as unfinished. A dropped `postgres` leaves the `knobas` database (OID 16384 or above), and one
  in a tablespace leaves an entry under `pg_tblspc/`. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **The answering-server check is not a data guard.** *Fork:* add a live-pid test to `served` for
  a postmaster in the instant between writing `postmaster.pid` and binding (#1789's window), or
  not. *Ruling:* not. *Reasoning:* `served` is read only for a directory that holds no database,
  and this build starts no server on one: it removes it first, and its own `initdb` leaves
  `base/5`. A postmaster an older build left in that instant loses files that hold no reader's
  data. A pid test would bring back the recycled-pid lockout #1789 removed. *Reversing:* one
  function.
- **A data directory copied in during a launch.** *Fork:* guard against a copy that has reached
  `base/1` but not the rest, or not. *Ruling:* not. *Reasoning:* a copy or a move across volumes
  keeps its source until it finishes, and a move within one is a rename, so nothing the reader
  has is lost. *Reversing:* n/a.
## #1641: the rebinding guard, an adapter's log, https for a release (Opus implementer, 2026-10-23)

- **Where the guard's ranges come from.** *Fork:* std's `is_global` list, or the registries.
  *Ruling:* the IANA IPv4 and IPv6 special-purpose registries as published on 2025-10-09, read
  by their "Globally Reachable" column, with multicast (`224/4`, `ff00::/8`) added and IPv6
  outside `2000::/3` refused. *Reasoning:* `is_global` is still unstable; the registries are
  what it is written from, and an allow rule for IPv6 (only global unicast is public) cannot miss
  a block IANA adds outside it. *Reversing:* low, two tables in `allow.rs`.
- **Documentation addresses (`192.0.2/24`, `198.51.100/24`, `203.0.113/24`, `2001:db8::/32`,
  `3fff::/20`).** *Fork:* public or not. *Ruling:* not public, as the registry says. Nothing
  public answers there, so a fixed name that resolves to one is no host the adapter needs. The
  network tests' stand-in public address moves from `203.0.113.7` to `1.1.1.1`; no test connects
  to it. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **Entries the registry leaves without a value.** TEREDO (`2001::/32`, "N/A") is refused: it is
  inside `2001::/23`, which is not reachable "unless allowed by a more specific allocation", and
  TEREDO is not so allowed. The terminated 6to4 relay block (`192.88.99.0/24`) stays public but
  for `192.88.99.2/32`, which the registry marks not reachable. 6to4 (`2002::/16`, "N/A") is
  read as the IPv4 address in its bits 16 to 47, as the ticket says. *Reversing:* low.
- **NAT64.** `64:ff9b::/96` is the IPv4 address in its low 32 bits. The local-use
  `64:ff9b:1::/48` is refused whole (the registry marks it not reachable). A network's own NAT64
  prefix (RFC 6052 §2.2) cannot be told from the address and counts as what it is: a gap no
  address check closes, named in `is_public`'s doc. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **IPv4-compatible `::a.b.c.d`.** *Fork:* read it as the IPv4 address (as before) or refuse it.
  *Ruling:* refuse: it is outside `2000::/3`, deprecated since RFC 4291, and no host answers it.
  IPv4-mapped `::ffff:a.b.c.d` is still the IPv4 address. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **The log's bound.** *Fork:* the numbers. *Ruling:* 4 KiB a line, 100 lines a call, then one a
  second, counted and reported as one warn line when the component writes again or the store is
  dropped. *Reasoning:* a call may run up to `MAX_DEADLINE` (an hour), which keeps the worst call
  under 15 MiB of log; a well-behaved adapter writes a handful of lines a call. *Reversing:*
  trivial, three constants in `limits.rs`.
- **The refill is witnessed by a unit test, not the flood.** The fixture's 1,000-line flood ends
  in about 0.2 s, inside the burst, so the end-to-end test bounds the burst and the cut; the
  one-a-second refill is held by `limits::tests::a_call_logs_its_burst_then_one_line_a_second`
  over explicit instants. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **What counts as "this machine" for plain http.** *Ruling:* a loopback address
  (`127.0.0.0/8`, `::1`) or the name `localhost`, which resolvers keep on loopback (RFC 6761).
  `localhost.` and `*.localhost` are not. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **Beyond `Origin::parse`.** *Fork:* the pasted URL only, as the ticket names, or every fetch.
  *Ruling:* every fetch of a release refuses a non-https URL off this machine, and so does a
  URL the answer came from after any redirects (a hop between the two is not checked: #1830,
  merge-manager review). *Reasoning:* a release API's answer names the asset URLs and a download
  redirects; checking only what was pasted leaves both on whatever scheme the server answers.
  *Reversing:* low, two checks in `remote::get`.
- **A GitHub repository URL over http.** *Ruling:* accepted: nothing is fetched from it, and its
  release is read through `Endpoints::github_api` (https). *Reversing:* trivial.
- **An adapter installed earlier from a plain-http URL.** Its update check and update now fail
  with the https message, and so does a restore that has to fetch it again. *Ruling:* intended;
  the reader re-installs it from an https URL. Booked in
  `docs/contract/10.8/1641-a-release-is-fetched-over-https.md`. *Reversing:* low.

### #1641, merge-manager review (Opus, 2026-10-23)

- **The range tables.** *Fork:* accept the two tables or correct an entry. *Ruling:* accept.
  Checked line by line against the IPv4 and IPv6 special-purpose registries (2025-10-09): every
  entry marked not globally reachable is in `NOT_PUBLIC_V4`, `NOT_PUBLIC_V6` or outside
  `2000::/3`, and every entry marked reachable inside a refused block (`192.0.0.9`, `192.0.0.10`;
  `2001:1::1`–`3`, `2001:3::/32`, `2001:4:112::/48`, `2001:20::/28`, `2001:30::/28`) is in
  `PUBLIC_V4` or `PUBLIC_V6`. *Reversing:* low.
- **The implementer's calls on unclear entries.** *Ruling:* all four upheld. TEREDO refused: a
  public host does not live on a Teredo address, and its client half is obfuscated, so no
  carried-address reading is safe. `192.88.99.0/24` public but for `.2`: that is the registry's
  own split. IPv4-compatible `::a.b.c.d` refused. The local-use NAT64 `64:ff9b:1::/48` refused
  whole and not unmapped: a local translator may map it onto the reader's own network, and the
  registry marks it not reachable. *Reversing:* trivial each.
- **`localhost` over plain http is judged by its name, not its resolved address.** *Fork:*
  resolve and check that the peer is loopback, or drop the `localhost` allowance. *Ruling:* keep
  it as it is. *Reasoning:* the install fetch goes through knobas-http's system resolver, and
  RFC 6761 §6.3 keeps `localhost` off the wire. macOS answers it locally, as do `/etc/hosts` and
  systemd-resolved, so an on-path attacker gets no DNS query to poison. The wasm host's rebinding
  guard is a separate path and is not involved: it covers a component's own requests, not the
  install. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **An adapter installed earlier from plain http off this machine.** *Fork:* migrate the stored
  `source_url`, or let the update path fail. *Ruling:* let it fail, with no migration. *Reasoning:*
  the installed component keeps running and nothing stored changes. `check_adapter_updates`
  records the `NotHttps` message as the adapter's failed check, which the Settings list shows
  (`TfInstalledAdapters`). `update_adapter` answers `invalid` with the same message. Upgrading
  the URL to https silently would fetch from a server the reader never named. *Reversing:* low.
- **The redirect check sees the last URL only.** *Fork:* check every hop now, or file it.
  *Ruling:* file it as #1830 (`backlog`) and correct the wording in `remote::get` and the §10.8
  entry. *Reasoning:* knobas-http follows a GET's redirects with reqwest's default policy, so
  checking each hop means changing `crates/knobas-http/**`, which is another frozen surface and
  outside this ticket. The gap needs the release's own https server to redirect to plain http.
  *Reversing:* n/a.

## #1643 / PR #1826: implementer rulings (Opus implementer, 2026-10-23)

- **Reserved for Björn, ruled by implementer on Opus: `open_checkout`'s IPC arguments.** *Fork:*
  drop `command` outright, or keep it and validate the program against the saved list. *Ruling:*
  drop it, with no replacement argument; `application`, `file` and `line` stay as they were, and
  the §10.8 entry is `docs/contract/10.8/1643-open-checkout-takes-no-command-and-two-reads-clamp.md`.
  *Reasoning:* spec #1620 ruling C4 and ADR-0016: a program from a setting is only true when
  the command takes no program. A check against the list would be a second copy of the list's
  rules at the shim. *Reversing:* the argument, the `Run` enum and the entry come back.
- **What *Try it* does to the dialog.** *Fork:* after a try saves the draft, close the dialog, or
  keep it open; and on Cancel, keep the saved try or put the list back. *Ruling:* the dialog
  stays open and edits the entry the try saved (*Add application* then writes over it, not a
  second one); closing it unsaved saves the list and default back as they were before the first
  try. *Try it* needs a name now, as the save refuses one without. *Reasoning:* C4 calls the
  save "one extra write the reader does not see"; an application that stays in every menu after
  Cancel is one the reader sees. *Reversing:* `dismiss` in `TfAppDialog.svelte` calls `onclose`
  alone.
- **How the environment is scrubbed.** *Fork:* `env_remove` a fixed list of the variables knobas
  reads, or drop every `KNOBAS_*` name. *Ruling:* `env_clear` and pass the parent's environment
  back less every name starting `KNOBAS_`. The builder takes the parent environment as an
  argument, so the test hands it a `KNOBAS_DB_URL` without setting one in the test process.
  *Reasoning:* a fixed list misses the next variable somebody adds; `std::env::set_var` in a
  threaded test binary is unsound. *Reversing:* one filter.
- **Where the clamp sits.** *Fork:* in the `#[tauri::command]` itself, or in its `_inner` body.
  *Ruling:* in `room_suggestions_inner` and `list_entities_inner`, which are the shims' bodies,
  under a named `commands::ROW_CEILING` that `list_sync_runs` now reads too. *Reasoning:* a
  `#[tauri::command]` cannot be called from a test, and the criterion asks for a tested clamp.
  Every caller of the `_inner`s is a command or a test. *Reversing:* move two lines.
- **500 against the views that ask for 1000.** *Fork:* clamp `list_entities` at 500 as the ticket
  says, or at the 1000 that `TfCode`, `TfRepo`, `TfPr` and `TfCodeRow` ask for. *Ruling:* 500,
  per the criterion; filed #1825 (`ready-for-agent`) for the four views, which now draw at most
  500 rows of a larger mirror. *Reasoning:* a ruling may not contradict the ticket.
  *Reversing:* one constant, or paging in the four views (#1825).

## #1643 / PR #1826: merge-manager rulings (Opus merge-manager, 2026-10-23)

- **Reserved for Björn, ruled by implementer on Opus (`open_checkout` loses `command`): upheld.**
  Reviewed against ADR-0016 and C4: the shim, the `_inner`, the fake and `entity.ts` all drop the
  argument, and nothing in `app/src` still sends one. The generated mirror carries types only,
  not command arguments, so `just ipc-mirror` producing no change is right. *Reversing:* as the
  implementer's ruling.
- **The four views that ask `list_entities` for 1000 rows.** *Fork:* merge with the 500 clamp
  and #1825 as the follow-up, or keep the views whole in this PR. *Ruling:* keep them whole:
  `entity.ts`'s `listEntities` reads a limit past `ROW_CEILING` in reads of 500 from `offset`,
  up to `LIST_MOST` (1000), and drops a row a later read repeats. `ROW_CEILING` is declared in
  `entity.ts` and a Rust test holds it equal to `commands::ROW_CEILING`. *Reasoning:* the clamp
  is the ticket's (500, the one `list_sync_runs` uses), but a view that drew 1000 repositories
  yesterday and 500 today, with nothing saying so, is a regression this PR would ship; the
  pull request page finds its repository in that read, so a source with more than 500
  repositories would lose the header's checkout. Paging keeps every payload under the ceiling,
  and the 1000 cap keeps a miscomputed limit from reading a whole table in pieces. #1825 is
  narrowed to the truncation past 1000, which predates this PR. *Reversing:* `listEntities`
  goes back to one `invoke`.
- **`TfPr`'s `room_suggestions` read of 1000.** *Ruling:* 500, unpaged. *Reasoning:*
  `room_suggestions` takes no offset, and Review reads the same room at 500 (`REVIEW_LIMIT`), so
  the pull request page now marks the proposals Review lists. Named in #1825. *Reversing:* an
  offset on `room_suggestions`, a §10.8 change.
- **Closing the dialog after *Try it* saves the old list back.** *Fork:* is that a lost edit or
  a race that overwrites a newer save? *Ruling:* neither, no change. *Reasoning:* Cancel
  discarded a try before this PR too (the try saved nothing), so putting the list back keeps
  what Cancel meant; *Add application* and *Save* clear the snapshot, so a confirmed save is
  never undone. Inside the dialog *Save*, *Add* and *Try it* are disabled while the try's save is
  in flight, so the restore is ordered after it. The one race left is a second whole-list save
  (a ↑ or a new default in *Manage applications*) sent in the milliseconds between Cancel and
  the try's answer; that is the same last-writer-wins property two fast ↑ clicks already have,
  and no person clicks inside it. *Reversing:* serialise `Apps.save`.
- ***Try it* is disabled until a name and a command are typed (prototype-6 always enables
  it).** *Ruling:* keep it, a departure from prototype-6 named here as the conventions ask.
  *Reasoning:* *Try it* now saves, and the save refuses an entry with no name; the button
  shares *Add application*'s `ready`, which the dialog already drew disabled for the same
  reason, and it was already disabled with no command before this PR. *Reversing:* enable it
  and show the save's refusal in the dialog.
