## Björn's request, 2026-10-24: fix a small follow-up in place (implementer, Opus, 2026-10-24)

Björn: "try not to create so many backlog tickets, tell the implementers to try and fix the issue themselves if it's not too big of an impact." One pass checking the 2026-10-22 review's fixes had filed 17 issues (#1973, #1975–#1989). No issue; a direct request.

- **What "not too big an impact" means.** *Ruling:* five conditions, all required: about 100 changed lines or fewer added to the PR's diff, tests included; no frozen surface the PR wasn't already touching (the merge-manager's deep-pass list); no change to what `scripts/gate-scope.sh` prints; no decision reserved for Björn; no app change he would need to judge that no ticket asked for. *Reasoning:* each is one a worker can check from its own diff. The gate-scope condition was added to the dispatch's list because a Rust fix folded into a frontend-only PR turns its `check-front` gate into a full one and sends a worker the brief told to run no cargo into a workspace build. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **Instance or class.** *Ruling:* the whole class has to fit; otherwise nothing is fixed and the class is filed. *Reasoning:* *Filing a follow-up* already says to file the class. Fixing the one instance in front of the worker and filing the rest splits one cause across a fix and an issue, and the issue's instance list goes stale at once. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **What the PR says.** *Ruling:* a **Fixed in passing** heading, one line per fix (what, `path:line`, the test), and each fix in its own commit with a test that fails without it; prose needs none. An open issue for the same cause is closed by the PR only when every instance it lists is fixed. *Reasoning:* the merge-manager reviews a folded fix as part of the PR, so it has to be findable and tested like the ticket's own code. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **The merge-manager's side.** *Ruling:* the same test; a fix that passes it is pushed onto the branch before the merge and counts toward the 3-round cap. Review step 5's "out-of-scope fixes: report with the finding quoted" now covers only what fails the test. *Reasoning:* the merge-manager already fixes on the branch; the cap keeps a folded fix from holding a merge open. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **`ticket-loop.md`'s *Issues you file*.** *Ruling:* kept, with a sentence after it: the workers fix before they file, and a checking pass the orchestrator dispatches outside a ticket (the kind that filed the 17) gets the same default in its prompt and fixes what passes in one self-merge PR. The milestone reviewer keeps "never fix anything yourself". *Reasoning:* the grep over `.claude/` and `docs/agents/` (`grep -rn -i "review\|file each\|never fix"`) found no brief for a fix-checking pass; such passes are prompts the orchestrator writes, so the rule goes where it writes them. The milestone reviewer certifies code it wrote none of, and its gaps block a release, so they are not backlog. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **A folded fix on a self-merge PR (found by the Standards review).** *Ruling:* on a *self-merge* dispatch the fit test also keeps the PR inside the loop's self-merge limits (no live suite, under ~150 lines, docs-only stays docs-only), and a checking pass whose PR outgrows *Self-merge* gets a merge-manager. *Reasoning:* otherwise a folded fix could carry a PR past the line that decided nobody reviews it. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **The 100 lines count every folded fix together**, and the bullet is *The fit test* so it isn't read against *Filing a follow-up*'s *The test*. A wrong ticket, spec, ADR or glossary line stays with *Decisions* (follow it, file the conflict), not this rule. *Reversing:* trivial.

## #1978: a worklog draft is read with the day offset it is logged with (implementer, Opus, 2026-10-24)

- **Where the Day tab test lives.** *Fork:* keep it at the App seam (`App.test.svelte.ts`, which `testenv/desktop-witness-test.sh` pins, so the head takes the full gate), or move `draftFor` into a module to test it under the front gate. *Ruling:* the App seam. *Reasoning:* the ticket's criterion is the request *Log…* sends, and `App.test.svelte.ts` already drives it through the real Day tab; a module made only to dodge the pin moves the code for the gate's sake. No Rust changes, so the full gate costs time, not risk. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **Both clock changes, not only October's.** *Ruling:* each test runs on 2026-10-25 (midnight +120) and 2026-03-29 (midnight +60). *Reasoning:* on one day alone, a mutant that sends today's offset survives whenever today shares that day's midnight offset, as it does today; the pair kills it in either season. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **`ReaderDay.offsetMinutes`'s doc (found by the ticket's grep).** *Ruling:* it now names `dayOffsetMinutes(day)`, not `offsetMinutes()`. *Reasoning:* it told the next caller to compute the offset at any instant, the cause of this ticket. The file is a Rust-included IPC mirror, but its check reads only `invoke<` call sites. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **One `readerDay(day)` for every caller (the Standards review's Data Clump, fixed here under Björn's 2026-10-24 small-follow-up rule).** *Fork:* leave six call sites building `{ day, offsetMinutes }` by hand, or route them through one helper. *Ruling:* `readerDay(day)` in `lib/time/day.ts`; `App.svelte`, `drafting.svelte.ts`, `TfWorklogDraft.svelte`, `TfLogAll.svelte`, `tf/time/day-read.ts` and `AdHocBlock.svelte` call it, and `ReaderDay`'s doc names it. *Reasoning:* the bug was two of six hand-built pairs picking another hour; one function makes the midnight offset a single choice rather than a convention. 46 lines, no visible change. *Reversing:* trivial. `localDay` (`time/draft`) and `dayKey` (`time/day`) doing the same job, which the review also noted, predates this diff and is left as it is.
## #1975 and #1988: the identity and the Tickets words fold with the server's `lower()` (implementer, Opus, 2026-10-24)

- **The class, swept.** *Ruling:* every value the search binds against a `lower(...)` column is now bound as typed and folded by the server: `assigned:`'s usernames and the Tickets words (the two tickets), `has:`'s user, and the board's `review-for-me` user in `mini_board::SIGNALS`. *Reasoning:* the corpus notes say `has:` admits exactly the tickets whose cards show the signal, so folding `has:` on the server while the board kept Rust's fold would split them on `İ`, the split `signals_ipc` now pins. The rest already folded on the server: the six name keys, `under:`, `reach:`, `name:`, the suggestions and `known_parent_positions`. *Reversing:* cheap.
- **The words keep their typed spelling; the parity fixture keeps its folded one.** *Fork:* change `needle-parity.json` and `needles.ts` to typed spellings, or fold the Rust side's alternatives before comparing in the parity test. *Ruling:* the parity test folds. `word_alternatives` keeps the first spelling typed and drops a later one that `same_value` calls the same, the once-each rule `under:` follows. `needles()` (the marks) still lowercases. *Reasoning:* the browser's copy feeds only the `?fake-ipc` filter and the marks, both case-blind, so case was never part of what the two copies agree on. Leaving `app/` alone keeps the bug fix free of any visible change. *Reversing:* cheap.
- **The board folds with `array(select lower(u) from unnest($2))`, not one bind per name.** *Ruling:* `SIGNALS` is a `const` statement with one `text[]` bind, so the fold is a subquery run once per statement. *Reasoning:* `bind_lowered`'s one bind per value is for statements built per query, where the planner's estimate of a folded constant matters (`under:` over 100,000 items). The board's signal read is over the cards it already keeps. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **Exact identity compares are not this class.** *Ruling:* the inbox's `r.value = any($1)` and `i.author = any($1)`, `entity_list`'s `v.value = me.me`, the launcher's `author = any(...)` and the card's `mine` (`eq_ignore_ascii_case`) are left alone and nothing is filed. *Reasoning:* none of them compares through `lower()`, and the inbox's comments say the identity matches the username as the source spells it (#82), so that is a design choice and not this drift. *Reversing:* n/a.
## #1973: a start-work step held as unconfirmed (implementer, Opus, 2026-10-24)

- **What an unconfirmed step counts as.** *Fork:* keep it failed with new words, count it queued, or add a step outcome for it. *Ruling:* queued. `Landing::Unconfirmed` maps to `StepOutcome::Queued`, and the step's detail reads "sent, but <source> did not answer, so it may have arrived -- check <source>, then send it again or discard it in the write queue". *Reasoning:* Björn's #1966 ruling makes an unconfirmed hold count as on its way, and `queued` is the outcome that already means neither a success to act on nor a failure to retry. The sequence waits on it. A failed step's wording invites a second send of a transition that may have landed. A new outcome would change `knobas.start_work_step`'s stored values and the IPC's `StartWorkOutcome`, both §10.8 surfaces, for a fact the detail already carries. *Reversing:* cheap (one match arm).
- **The *Retry* button beside a queued step stays.** *Fork:* hide or relabel it for an unconfirmed step, or keep it. *Ruling:* kept. *Reasoning:* on a step whose write is still open, *Retry* re-reads that write and sends nothing (`ready_retry`'s rule 1, pinned by `a_transition_never_answered_is_on_its_way_and_its_retry_sends_nothing`). After the reader sends the write again from the queue, that re-read moves the step to succeeded. Hiding it would strand the step. The frontend cannot tell an unconfirmed queued step from a waiting one without a new IPC field, and relabelling *Retry* on every queued step is an app change no ticket asked for. *Reversing:* cheap.
- **Unconfirmed before source-off.** *Fork:* the write queue's panel says "source turned off" first for a held row whose source is off. *Ruling:* the step reads an unconfirmed send first, whether its source is on or off. *Reasoning:* whether the write may already be at the source decides whether a second send is safe, and turning the source off afterwards does not change that. `QueuedWrite::may_have_landed` ignores `source_enabled` for the same reason. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **A source-off hold (fixed in passing).** *Ruling:* `Landing::SourceOff`, still a failed step, worded as the panel words it: re-enable the source in Sources to send it, or discard it. *Reasoning:* it fell to the same "the target changed" sentence, which CONTEXT.md's *Held write* forbids ("the reasons are never collapsed"). Every hold but the unconfirmed one stays failed, so its outcome does not change. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **The merge follower.** *Ruling:* a merge's transition that lands unconfirmed counts as followed, with its activity line, as a queued one does. *Reasoning:* same #1966 ruling. It is never sent twice either way, because the queued row is `due`'s memory. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **Not a §10.8 entry.** *Ruling:* none booked. *Reasoning:* `Landing` never leaves the process. `StepOutcome`'s values and `FlowStep`'s shape are unchanged, and `detail` was already free text. *Reversing:* n/a.

## #1996 (#1973): the merge-manager's review (merge-manager, Opus, 2026-10-24)

- **The *Retry* beside a queued unconfirmed step.** *Fork:* relabel or hide it on the branch, or keep it and file the label. *Ruling:* kept on this PR, and the label is filed as #1998. *Reasoning:* the button sends nothing on an open write (`ready_retry`'s rule 1, pinned by `a_transition_never_answered_is_on_its_way_and_its_retry_sends_nothing`), so no second transition can go out from it, which is what #1973 and the #1966 ruling protect. It is also the only thing that moves the step on after *Send again* in the queue, since `run` stops at a queued step, so hiding it would strand the step. The label is still wrong: *Retry* beside "it may have arrived" reads as the second send. But the same button on a waiting step does the same re-read, so the honest fix relabels every queued step. That is an app change no ticket asked for, so it fails the fit test. *Reversing:* cheap.
- **Unconfirmed before source-off.** *Ruling:* kept as the implementer has it. *Reasoning:* the panel puts source-off first because it can't offer *Send again* while the source is off. That is a question of which button to show. The step's question is whether a second send is safe, and turning the source off doesn't change whether the first one arrived. Both orders keep the reasons apart. The unconfirmed step's "send it again or discard it in the write queue" takes the reader to the panel, and the panel then says to re-enable the source first. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **No §10.8 entry.** *Ruling:* confirmed. *Reasoning:* `Landing` derives only `Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq`, and no file outside `start_work/` names it. The new `knobas_core::write_queue::UnconfirmedSend` has no `Serialize` or `ts` derive. `QueuedWrite`, `StepOutcome`, `FlowStep` and the `detail` column are unchanged, and the diff adds no migration. *Reversing:* n/a.

## #1980: a sync knobas' own rate limit stopped sets no backoff (implementer, Opus, 2026-10-24)

- **Whether such a run counts in `failures_since_last_ok`.** *Ruling:* it does not, as a cancelled run does not (#1629). *Reasoning:* the source was not asked. Counted, five quota stops in a row would put the source's next real failure on the top rung (60 min) at once, which is the backoff for a wait knobas imposed that the ticket rules out, only one run later. `a_run_stopped_on_the_local_quota_sets_no_backoff` pins the first rung after one. *Reversing:* cheap (one SQL line).
- **How the row says so.** *Fork:* a column (a migration), a field on `RunResult` (the ladder reads the log, so it needs the row to carry it anyway), matching `LocalQuota`'s `Display` in SQL, or a prefix knobas-sync owns. *Ruling:* `run_log::LOCAL_QUOTA_PREFIX` ("stopped on knobas' own rate limit, not the source: ") ahead of the failure's message, which `RunResult::stopped_on_local_quota` and `failures_since_last_ok` read. *Reasoning:* `CANCELLED_MESSAGE` is the same move for the same reason (`outcome` is a checked column and an IPC type). The prefix is written only when the watch marked the run, never read off an adapter's words, and every `SyncError` display starts with its own prefix, so an adapter's message cannot produce it. Matching `knobas-http`'s `Display` would tie the ladder to another crate's wording. *Reversing:* cheap.
- **What the watch covers.** *Ruling:* the sync call alone (`run_from_stored_cursor`/`run_backfill`), not the adapter build or field discovery. *Reasoning:* the build runs on `spawn_blocking`, where the task-local is not seen, and sends nothing; discovery's failure is skipped, not the run's, and a quota stop there would otherwise mark a run that later failed on something else. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **Which failure the mark turns into a quota stop.** *Ruling:* a `SyncError::Source(Protocol { status: None, .. })` with the mark set, the write queue's `retryable` test. *Reasoning:* the mark is the call's, last one wins, so a sync whose adapter swallowed one quota stop and then failed `Unreachable` or with a status still backs off. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **The credential verdict.** *Ruling:* judged like any error run: a stored `unreachable` is cleared (#1477), any other state left alone. *Reasoning:* the quota stop is what the row now says, and a stale `unreachable` drawn over it is #1477's bug. Only the backoff is knobas' own business here. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **The class, checked.** *Ruling:* nothing else changed. *Reasoning:* the callers that map an error to health or backoff are `apply_health_and_backoff` (fixed), the write queue (reads the mark since #1729; its build path passes `None`, correctly, since a build sends nothing) and `sources::crud::set_secret`'s re-test, which writes `unreachable` health for every `Protocol` by design ("knobas could not talk to it", which is true of a quota stop) and never sets a backoff. *Test connection* (draft) and discovery write nothing. The wasm host's wait never fails with `LocalQuota`. Search: `grep -rn "set_health\|set_backoff\|clear_unreachable\|failures_since_last_ok\|backs_off()" crates --include=*.rs`. *Reversing:* n/a.

## #1980 review: the quota mark, the boxed sync and the shared predicate (merge-manager, Opus, 2026-10-24)

- **Can an adapter's message forge `LOCAL_QUOTA_PREFIX`?** *Ruling:* no; the prefix and the `starts_with` in `failures_since_last_ok` stay. *Reasoning:* every other message the scheduler logs opens with a tag knobas writes: `SyncError`'s `source:`, `database:`, `source id`, `source "…"`; `SourceError`'s `unauthorized`, `unreachable:`, `unconfirmed:`, `protocol:`, `sink:`, `moved:` for a build failure; `keychain:`, the missing-secret, no-config, cancelled and run-stopped constants. An adapter's words only ever follow one of those tags. *Reversing:* cheap.
- **The boxed sync future.** *Ruling:* keep. *Reasoning:* one heap allocation per run, next to a database connection and a network sync. The `Send` bound is what the scheduler's spawn needs anyway, and it is what holds `knobas-app`'s future under the query depth. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **The real-clock test with a 200 ms budget.** *Ruling:* keep. *Reasoning:* the ticket names the 200 ms. The only thing on the wall clock is the first loopback round trip, and `knobas-http`'s transport suite (200 ms) and `write_queue.rs` (50 ms) already run tighter budgets on the same clock in the gate. If load ever breaks it, it fails loudly with `Unreachable`; it cannot pass by accident. It passed three runs out of three at a one-minute load of 19 on 12 cores. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **Share the quota predicate with `write_queue::retryable`?** *Ruling:* no, not in this PR; a one-line comment at the scheduler's match names `retryable` as its twin. *Reasoning:* the predicate is one match arm. Sharing it would edit the write queue, a frozen surface this PR does not touch otherwise, so it fails the fit test. Two copies of one arm are not a class worth a ticket either. *Reversing:* cheap.
- **External (wasm) adapters, which the ticket's failure scenario names.** *Ruling:* out of reach, and accepted rather than filed. *Reasoning:* the #1631 ruling (#1728 and #1631, 2026-10-22) bounds the host's limiter wait by the call's deadline alone, so an external adapter's request waits for its token and never fails on the quota. The case that is left, a wait that runs into the deadline, is #1729's question, already answered there. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **The prefix shows in the diagnostics view's error line.** *Ruling:* keep. The Spec axis called it beyond the ticket. *Reasoning:* the ticket asks the PR to decide whether such a run counts on the ladder, and the ladder reads the log, so the row has to carry the mark. The words are true, they say why no backoff followed, and `CANCELLED_MESSAGE` is the precedent. *Reversing:* cheap.
## #1981 and #1982: the Bash guard reads a leading redirection, and its wiring takes the full gate (implementer, Opus, 2026-10-24)

- **A redirection is a word of its own kind.** *Ruling:* the parser marks a redirection (`>`, `<`, `&>`, `<>`, `<<<`, a heredoc), with an fd number or `{fd}` glued before it, as `Word.redirect`; the name skips it, the arguments leave it out, and only it names a write target. *Reasoning:* skipping words that *look* like redirections in `name_and_args` would also skip a quoted `'>x'`, and the text test it replaces refused `echo '>.git/x'`, which writes nothing. *Reversing:* cheap.
- **`&>` no longer splits a command.** *Ruling:* `&>` and `&>>` are redirections, not `&` then `>`. *Reasoning:* `cd /tmp &>/dev/null` read as two commands and was refused as a chained cd; bash runs one. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **The ticket's lower-priority shapes.** *Ruling:* fixed, with tests: a shell with no script operand (or `-s`) runs the last heredoc or here-string fed to it; `find`'s `-exec`, `-execdir`, `-ok` and `-okdir` commands are read up to `;` or `+`; a `case` pattern's `)` closes no substitution. A script piped into a shell (`echo '…' | bash`) is named in the guard's header as a known gap. *Reasoning:* each fix is under 20 lines; a pipe's left side prints what the guard cannot know without running it. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **A heredoc stands in its command as a word, with or without substitutions in its body.** *Ruling:* so `bash <<EOF` can read its body; `<<EOF` alone on a line is now a command, as bash reads it (a null command with a redirection), so a later `cd` on its own line counts as chained. *Reasoning:* bash does the same; no transcript has the shape. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **#1982: scope `.claude/` non-Markdown `full`, not run the guard's test from `docs-check`.** *Fork:* the ticket's two options. *Ruling:* `gate-scope.sh` drops `.claude/*` from its prose paths (Markdown anywhere is still prose through `*.md`), and `ticket-loop.md`'s docs-only list names `.claude/` Markdown only. *Reasoning:* one rule in one script, which the full `check` (with `witness-unit`, so `bash-guard-test.sh`) already follows; `docs-check` stays a seconds-long prose check, and `.claude/loop/stages.sh`, a script the other option would have left as prose, takes the full gate too. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **`gate-scope-test.sh` ignores the machine's global excludes file.** *Ruling:* its scratch repo runs git with `core.excludesFile=/dev/null`. *Reasoning:* `~/.config/git/.gitignore` ignores `.claude/*`, so the scratch repo never tracked `.claude/commands/loop.md` and the case could not run. *Reversing:* trivial.
## #1983: the store-reset check sees every module-level store shape (implementer, Opus, 2026-10-24)

- **Which declarations count as a store.** *Ruling:* a column-0 `const` or `let` made by `$state`, a `create…()` factory, or `new` of `Map`, `Set`, `WeakMap`, `WeakSet`, `Date`, `URL` or `URLSearchParams` (bare or `Svelte…`), and any column-0 `let` except one that starts at a number. *Reasoning:* those are the mutable shapes the store files use. A `let` that starts at a number is an id counter (`toasts`' `nextId`, `pending-comments`' `counter`), which keeps counting across tests on purpose (#1762). A `const` object or array literal is left out: in the store files every one is a constant table or a port bundle, and the shape can't tell them apart. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **A component's `<script module>` is scanned too.** *Fork:* reset the three pages' session memory (`TfBuilds#remembered`, `TfRepo#chosen`, `TicketsPage#session`) through the components, or move the stores into `.svelte.ts` files that are cheaper to import. *Ruling:* through the components, reading the module script at its own indent. *Reasoning:* the TF conventions keep a page's session switches "as the page's module `$state`" (the Tickets line), so stores live there by design. The cost is that each test file loads the three page modules in its first reset. *Reversing:* cheap.
- **Plain `.ts` files stay unscanned, and `UNSCANNED` keeps listing what they hold.** *Reasoning:* outside `dev/`, their column-0 `new Set([...])`s are constant lookup tables (17 of them, `open-external.ts#ALLOWED` and `address.ts#ROOM_KINDS` among them), so this scan would flag every one. The `?fake-ipc` backend's module state under `shell/dev/fake/` stands in for the server, not for a window store. It fails the fit test (about 30 declarations), so it is filed as #2004. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **The read-aheads in flight go with the memory.** *Ruling:* `ViewMemory.clear()` also drops that memory's entry in `view-read.ts#flights`. *Reasoning:* the alternative was a second door just for tests. Left in place, a read still pending from one test answers the next test's read of the same entity, and the only caller of `clear()` is the test reset. *Reversing:* trivial.
## #1987: a tab switch on a job page reads nothing again (implementer, Opus, 2026-10-24)

- **The ticket says the job page does not re-read; it did.** *Ruling:* fixed here as part of the ticket, since the criterion counts every read through the job ports. *Reasoning:* on the tree at `b239edbf`, one tab switch cost the shell one `listSources` and the job page three: `TfPage` spread `page.props(ctx)`, one object new on each change to the shell's context (the route, `lastJob`, `navJobId`), and Svelte reads a spread prop through that object, so `TfJob`'s effect keyed on `segment` re-ran on each and re-opened the job (state reset, `Opening PAY-231…` drawn again). *Reversing:* n/a.
- **Where the page fix goes.** *Fork:* `TfJob` keys its effect on a `$derived(segment)`, or `TfPage` hands each prop as its own signal. *Ruling:* `TfPage`. *Reasoning:* the spread is the cause, and it reaches every page's effect keyed on a prop (Docs, Builds, Deps read the job by key the same way); one fix in the frame covers the class for every prop whose value stays `===`: strings, booleans and the shell's shared objects. An array the route builds afresh (`rest`) still tells its readers on a route change, which is a change of address within that page. The keys are read once per page, which holds because every `page.ts` returns an object literal. *Reversing:* cheap.
- **The shell: stop replacing `lastJob`, not an early return in the nav job's effect.** *Ruling:* the `lastJob` effect keeps the object while the segment stays, read under `untrack`. *Reasoning:* an early return still runs the effect's cleanup, which marks a read in flight stale, so a tab switch before the first read answered would lose it. Keeping the object also stops every other reader of `lastJob` re-running. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **What "unchanged" compares.** *Ruling:* the segment, not the key. *Reasoning:* `#/job/tide:PAY-231` then `#/job/PAY-231` is the same key and another job (#1525); the new test pins it. *Reversing:* trivial.

## #1976 and #1979: offset walks a deletion or an edit can no longer step over (implementer, Opus, 2026-10-24)

- **Jira: no keyset, an anchored offset walk.** *Fork:* the tickets' default, a JQL keyset `id > N ORDER BY id`, or their fallback, a per-page total check. *Ruling:* neither. The walk keeps `ORDER BY created ASC, id ASC` and `startAt`, and asks every page after the first one row early, from the last issue read, and one row longer. A page is accepted only when its first row is an issue the walk has read, or it starts at `0`; otherwise the walk asks again from twice as far back. Rows met twice are handed out once (`crates/knobas-source-jira/src/walk.rs`). *Reasoning:* the keyset is refuted on the seeded Jira 10.3: `id` is an alias of `issuekey`, so `id > <OPS-77's id>` answers no PAY issue though every one has a higher id, and `id > 0` is refused (`A value with ID '0' does not exist`), so a keyset on a deleted issue could not ask at all. The per-page total check fails #1979's own probe: PAY-1 deleted and PAY-6 filed between two pages leave the total at 5, and offset 2 starts at PAY-4. Over an order no edit moves, an issue the walk has read sorts before every one it has not, so a page that opens on one has nothing unread before it. *Reversing:* the module and one call site; the old `PageWalk` over `Offset` is one line.
- **Ruling A5 amended: a shrinking total no longer fails the run.** *Ruling:* `refuse_a_shrunk_total` is gone, and A5 in `docs/decisions/2026-10-review-planning-rulings.md` carries an amendment line. *Reasoning:* the anchored walk makes a deletion cost a request or two instead of a failed run, which is the false failure #1979 names (a busy filtered source that fails every full sync). #1979's criterion for amending A5 is worded for a keyset; the anchored walk meets its intent (a deletion behind the cursor no longer fails the run), and the tests `an_issue_deleted_behind_the_walk_hides_no_unread_one` and `a_deletion_that_empties_the_next_page_hides_no_unread_one` pin it. *Reversing:* one branch, as A5 said.
- **The walk ends on a page that brings nothing past where it stood.** *Ruling:* an accepted page with no unread row and no row past the walk's position ends the walk, whatever its `total` claims; an empty page at `startAt` > 0 is not the end but a page that does not open on a read row. *Reasoning:* asked from the last issue read, the page that used to come back empty now holds that one issue; and a deletion can leave the next offset past the listing's new end while unread rows remain before it. `a_page_with_nothing_past_the_walk_ends_it_while_total_still_claims_more` keeps the old empty-page guard's job. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **`MAX_PAGES` counts requests.** *Ruling:* the asks from further back count toward the cap. *Reasoning:* the cap bounds what a mispaging server can cost, and what it costs is requests. A step back ends at offset `0` at worst, so it adds at most `log2` of the walk's position to one page; a walk with no deletion under it sends one request a page as before, each asking one row more than it brings. At the default page size the cap is about half a million issues instead of exactly. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **Confluence: `order by created asc, id asc`, for the incremental walk too.** *Fork:* #1976 lets the incremental walk keep `lastmodified`. *Ruling:* both use `created asc, id asc`; the time bound stays on `lastmodified`, the ceiling probe on `lastmodified desc`, and the mention walk on `lastmodified asc`. *Reasoning:* one order is one renderer, and an incremental walk over `lastmodified` steps over a page the same way: the stepped-over page sits below the advanced watermark and waited for the next full sync. The mention walk delivers no kind the sweep reads (the page walk delivers every page). Data Center 9.2 accepts the order (`live_confluence_seeded`'s `a_cql_range_on_id_is_refused_and_the_walks_order_is_not`) and refuses `id >` (`Operator '>' is not supported for field 'id'`), so Confluence has no keyset either. *Reversing:* one string in `cql.rs`.
- **Confluence's anchored walk keeps the server's word on where the listing ends.** *Ruling:* the walk ends on a result with no `_links.next`, follows an empty result that has one, and takes the next offset from the result's own `start` plus `limit` (the server's clamp applied), not from the rows that arrived. *Reasoning:* that is what `NextLink` promised (an empty page with a link is followed), and the probe shows the server echoes `start`, `limit` and `totalSize` and builds its next link as `start + limit`. The page walk now sends `start` itself; the mention walk, the positions sweep and the re-read still follow `_links.next`. *Reversing:* the walk module.
- **Gitea: two listings on a full sync, not a per-page total check.** *Fork:* the dispatch's two options for an endpoint with no keyset. *Ruling:* a full sync lists `/repos/search` twice and walks the union (the selection is already deduplicated by name); an incremental run lists once. *Reasoning:* a total check misses a repository deleted while another is created in the same gap, as Jira's did, and fails the run on a deletion from a page not yet read. The union misses a repository only when a second deletion lands on the same row in the second listing. A repository listed by the first and gone by the second answers 404 when walked and is skipped as deleted since the listing, as before. An incremental run licenses no sweep; a repository its listing missed keeps no position for one run and is read whole the next. The listing is `ceil(n / 50)` requests against several per repository walked. *Reversing:* one loop bound.
- **The anchored walk lives in each adapter, not in `knobas-http`.** *Fork:* one walker beside `PageWalk` in the transport, or one per adapter. *Ruling:* one per adapter (`knobas-source-jira/src/walk.rs`, `knobas-source-confluence/src/walk.rs`). *Reasoning:* `crates/knobas-http/**` is on §10.8's frozen list and these tickets touch no frozen surface; the two copies differ where their products do (Jira's `total` ends a walk, Confluence's `_links.next` does). `PageWalk`'s module docs already name the walk that re-reads its listing as its adapter's own. Lifting it is a §10.8 entry and a follow-up if a third adapter needs one. *Reversing:* moderate.
- **What the sweep of the other adapters found.** *Ruling:* no other full-sync-exhaustive walk is paged by offset over an order a change can shift, except the Jira board listing, filed as #2003. TeamCity's two kinds are not exhaustive; Kuma reads its monitor list in one socket event; Gitea's branch listing already reads every name from git when it spans pages (#1716); the Confluence positions sweep and mention walk deliver nothing the sweep reads. The Jira board listing (`views::listing`, `startAt` over the agile API's own order, 50 a page) feeds `jira_view`, which is exhaustive and whose `gone` items tombstone a board missing from a run, so a board deleted from a page already read hides the next one for a run. *Reasoning:* it fails the fit test for an in-place fix: the agile listing's order is unmeasured, and the board fake serves a fixed list that would need a mutable listing and 51 boards to show it. *Reversing:* n/a.

## #1976 and #1979, merge review of #2006 (merge-manager, Opus, 2026-10-24)

- **The Jira walk's end rule, corrected.** *Fork:* end on any accepted page that brings nothing past the walk's position (the implementer's ruling above), or only on one asked from the anchoring row. *Ruling:* the walk ends there only when the request started one row back, or at offset `0` of an empty listing. An answer asked from further back that holds only rows already read stopped at its limit (`MAX_PAGE_SIZE`) or at the server's own clamp (`jira.search.views.default.max`), so the walk goes on from that answer's last row (`crates/knobas-source-jira/src/walk.rs`). *Reasoning:* a step back reaches between `d` and `2d` rows behind the walk for `d` rows deleted, and the rows read past the anchor fill the whole answer once they reach the clamp. The old rule then ended the walk `Ok` with every row past it unread, and the sweep tombstoned them: twelve issues, a clamp of three, four deleted after eight were read, and PAY-9 to PAY-12 were lost (`a_step_back_answered_short_of_the_walk_ends_nothing`, red before the fix; `a_listing_emptied_under_the_walk_ends_it` pins the offset-0 branch). With the defaults (page size 100, clamp 1,000) it takes about a thousand rows leaving behind the cursor between two pages. A bulk transition under a `resolution = Unresolved` filter does that. Confluence's walk is not affected: it ends only where no `_links.next` comes back. *Reversing:* one branch.
- **Ruling A5's amendment and the contract section are within an agent's authority.** *Ruling:* kept as the implementer wrote them, with a pointer added under A1, whose reasoning leaned on A5. *Reasoning:* spec #1618 waives Björn's gate for its batch ("the implementer on Opus rules what comes up and records it"). #1979's own criteria ask for A5 to be amended in `docs/decisions/`. The contract change only adds amendments, and no §10.8 path is touched (`crates/knobas-http/**` and `crates/knobas-source/src/**` are outside the diff). *Reversing:* the two amendment lines and the contract section.
- **Gitea's two listings, kept.** *Fork:* the union of two listings, or re-listing until two consecutive listings agree (#1979's other option). *Ruling:* the union of two. *Reasoning:* a repository is missed only when a second deletion lands before it during the second listing too. The harm lasts until the next run: the sweep's tombstone is lifted when the repository is listed again. The cost is `ceil(n / 50)` more requests on a full sync only, against several requests per repository walked. An agreement loop would add a set comparison and a cap for a case that rare. *Reversing:* the loop bound becomes a loop until two listings agree.
## #1985: a data directory an `initdb` killed before `PG_VERSION` left (Opus implementer, 2026-10-24)
## #1985: a data directory an `initdb` killed before `PG_VERSION` left (implementer, Opus, 2026-10-24)

- **Reproduce first.** *Fork:* reproduce it, or close the ticket because the state cannot arise. *Ruling:* reproduced, and it is the commonest state a cut-short cleanup leaves on a Mac. *Reasoning:* with PostgreSQL 18.6 on this Mac (scripts `issue-1985-cleanup-kill*.py` in that run's scratchpad), `initdb` refuses `data/` holding `base/` and `global/` alone: *exists but is not empty*. The new test was red on main with that error. Forty runs sent `initdb` a `SIGTERM`, then a `SIGKILL` as soon as its cleanup had removed `postgresql.conf`. Twenty were sent the `SIGTERM` once `global/pg_control` existed, and each left `base/1`, an empty `pg_tblspc/` and no `PG_VERSION` or `postgresql.conf`. Twenty were sent it once `base/5` existed, and each left `base/1`, `4` and `5`. Its `rmtree` removes entries in `readdir` order. On APFS `ls -f` lists `PG_VERSION` and `postgresql.conf` early and `global/` and `base/` last. Knobas sends that `SIGTERM` when `initdb` times out. A drop during `INITDB_GRACE`, or a quit, kills the cleanup. The window before `PG_VERSION` (the subdirectories, `base/1` among them, are made first) is microseconds wide, but a kill there leaves the same shape. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **What may be removed.** *Fork:* every non-empty directory without `PG_VERSION` or `postgresql.conf`, or only one that holds no database. *Ruling:* only one that holds no database. That means nothing under `base/` but `1`, `4` and `5`, and nothing under `pg_tblspc/`, and either directory may be missing. Like the other arms, removal skips a directory a postmaster answers for (`served`). *Reasoning:* the reader's data lives in the `knobas` database (an OID from 16384 up) or a tablespace, and a launch creates them only on a cluster a server ran on. `base/5` is allowed here, unlike in the `PG_VERSION` arm, because the cleanup leaves it behind; without `PG_VERSION` no server ever started on it, so `postgres` holds nothing. A missing `base/` or `pg_tblspc/` is the normal case here, not a doubt: the kill came before `initdb` made it, or after the cleanup removed it. The ticket's "never delete a directory that has `PG_VERSION`" holds: this arm only sees directories without one. A copy being made into `data/` that has no `PG_VERSION` and no `base/` yet is removed too, unlike in the `PG_VERSION` arm, where a missing `base/` is a doubt. What is lost there is the partial copy, not its source. *Reversing:* one predicate in `shape`.
- **A directory without `PG_VERSION` that may hold a database.** *Fork:* mark it, as `HoldsDatabase` is marked, or keep it unmarked. *Ruling:* a new `Shape::Unrecognised`, kept as it is, unmarked, with a warning in the log. `initdb` then refuses it as before. A `base/` that cannot be listed counts as a database. *Reasoning:* a marker would stop any later build from ever recovering it, and nothing in knobas made such a directory. *Reversing:* low.
- **The class.** *Fork:* fix the new state alone, or walk every shape. *Ruling:* walked every shape. Marked: written only after `initdb` succeeds. A kill while it is being written leaves no marker and `base/5`, so the next launch marks it. Not initialised: absent or empty, and `initdb` takes it. `postgresql.conf` without `PG_VERSION`: removed (#1637). Neither, not empty: this ticket. `PG_VERSION` with `base/` holding `1` or `1` and `4`: removed (#1819). `PG_VERSION` with `base/5`: finished, and marked. On APFS no kill leaves anything else, because the cleanup removes `PG_VERSION` before `postgresql.conf` and before `base/`. On a filesystem that lists the entries in another order (Linux ext4 lists by hash), a cut-short cleanup can leave `PG_VERSION` with `postgresql.conf` or `base/` already gone. Recovering that state means removing a `PG_VERSION` directory, which the ticket rules out ("Never delete a directory that has `PG_VERSION`"). It fails the fit test, so it is filed as #2007 (`backlog`; not witnessed, since no Linux machine was available). On Windows `terminate` is a no-op, so the cleanup never runs. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **Test seams.** *Fork:* confirm the seams with Björn first, as the TDD skill asks, or pick them. *Ruling:* picked, as in #1819: `EmbeddedDb::start` for what a launch does (the ticket's `base/` and `global/` fixture, plus the two states the kills left), and `shape` and `recover_or_mark` for the cases no launch sets up (a database, an unreadable `base/`, an empty or absent directory). *Reasoning:* the loop runs unattended. *Reversing:* n/a.
## #1984: every mirror check reads the call site, not a quoted name anywhere (implementer, Opus, 2026-10-24)

- **How far the class goes.** *Fork:* the `sources` test alone, or every barrel pin a quoted name anywhere satisfies. *Ruling:* every Rust test that pins an `app/src/lib/ipc/*.ts` barrel by finding a quoted name anywhere in the file. That is the `sources`, `app` and `search` command lists (now `assert_mirrors`), the `time` and `assets` argument tests (they now read the call through `commands::mirror::invocation`, which skips comment lines as `invoked` does), the `EVENTS` names in `lib.rs` (read off `EVENTS`' code lines and compared as a whole list), and `entity.ts`' `ROW_CEILING` (matched as a whole line). *Reasoning:* each could be satisfied by a doc comment. Without the last one, the ticket's `grep -n 'MIRROR.contains('` criterion could not pass. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **`app`'s list is read off `lib.rs`, not `app.rs`'s attributes.** *Ruling:* that is how `assert_mirrors` reads it, as for every other module. *Reasoning:* `tests/it/wiring.rs`' `every_command_is_in_the_handler_list` already pins every declared command to the handler list, so the two together cover what the old self-scan did, and the reverse direction is new. *Reversing:* cheap.
- **The argument tests also match the value side** (`offset: when.offsetMinutes` passes for `offsetMinutes`). *Ruling:* filed as #2008, not fixed here. *Reasoning:* the cause is a different one (substring, not position), and this PR's diff is already near the self-merge size limit. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **`the_view_commands_are_invoked_by_their_names` keeps its name** though it now pins every `search` command, and stays in `ticket_views.rs`. *Fork:* rename or move it to `commands/search.rs`. *Ruling:* keep it as it is. *Reasoning:* `test-inventory.txt` and the frozen §10.8 ledger entry for #1329 cite it by name and place. *Reversing:* cheap.
## #1986: one spelling per clock, age and ticket key (implementer, Opus, 2026-10-24)

- **The conversation's older stamp.** *Fork:* `clockLabel`'s bare date (`2026-08-12`), or keep the clock. *Ruling:* keep the clock, as the named variant `stampLabel` in `lib/time/format.ts` (`2026-08-12 09:14`), built on `clockLabel` so the date and the today/yesterday words are its. *Reasoning:* prototype-6's thread writes every older comment as `2026-08-11 10:20`; two comments on one day are told apart by the clock. *Reversing:* low.
- **The last backup's older line.** *Fork:* keep `2 Oct 23:00`, or `stampLabel`. *Ruling:* `stampLabel`: `2026-10-02 23:00, 1 KB, in …`. *Reasoning:* prototype-6 only draws today's backup, so the month name was the code's own; it was the one clock in the shell spelled with a month, and a backup's time matters as a comment's does. *Reversing:* low, one call.
- **A source's *Sync runs* column (fixed in passing).** *Ruling:* `startedWords` is `stampLabel(…, bare)`, so yesterday's run reads `yesterday 10:00` (was `14 Oct 10:00`) and an older one `2026-10-12 10:00` (was `12 Oct 10:00`); today's stays `14:28` as prototype-6 draws it. *Reasoning:* the same today/yesterday clock written a fourth way, which the ticket's grep did not name; `—` for an unreadable instant stays. *Reversing:* low.
- **`age()`'s `38 min` against `minutesLabel`'s `38m`.** *Fork:* spell the age with `minutesLabel`, or keep `38 min` as a named variant. *Ruling:* the variant `ageLabel` (`38 min`, `2 h`, `3 days`), and `shell/time.ts`'s `ago` builds its words under a day from it. *Reasoning:* an age is not a timesheet length. Prototype-6 writes *data is 38 min old* beside the status bar's *sign-in failed 38 min ago*, and `ago` already said `4 min ago`, so `38m old` would have opened a new divergence on the same screen. With `ago` on `ageLabel` the words exist once. No visible string changes. *Reversing:* low.
- **What the key-split rule scans.** *Ruling:* a house rule in `shell/house-rules.test.ts` refuses `.slice(<x>.indexOf(":") + 1)` and `.split(":")[1]` / `.split(":").pop()` in any non-test module but `format.ts`, the `?fake-ipc` backend included. *Reasoning:* the ticket asks for the expression, not the name; the backend builds the keys the surfaces read back (eight copies on surfaces, fourteen in the backend). Forms that also need the colon's index (`namespaceOf`, `repoOf`, a token's `key:value`) are left alone: they split a namespace off, not a key. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **`inbox.svelte.ts`'s `subjectOf` and the Code section's repo fallback.** *Ruling:* `subjectOf` stays (its test reads it) and delegates to `keyOf`; `TfCodeSection`'s `split(":").pop()` becomes `keyOf`, which differs only for a repository key with a colon in it, where it now keeps the whole key. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **The interval words.** *Ruling:* not touched. *Reasoning:* a schedule's period has one spelling the app draws, `intervalWords` (Settings, `15 min`, `1 hour`); `sources/diagnostics.ts`'s `formatInterval` (`every 15 min`) has no caller outside its test since the rooms UI went, so no page shows a second one. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **The key-split rule's `split(":")` arm (merge-manager, Opus).** *Fork:* refuse `.split(":")[1]` / `.split(":").pop()` on any receiver, or only on one named as an id. *Ruling:* only on a receiver named as an id (`…_id`, `…Id`, `id`, `entity`), pinned by *the key-split rule reads an id's split, not a clock's*; the `.slice(x.indexOf(":") + 1)` arm stays receiver-blind. *Reasoning:* a clock's minutes (`clock.split(":")[1]`) and a filter token's value are split the same way and are not keys, so the broad arm would fail the build on correct code with a message naming `keyOf`; both split copies the PR found were on `entity_id` receivers. The slice arm is the exact `keyOf` expression, whose receivers (`from`, `end`, `target`) carry no common name. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **The monitor chip's *down since* (merge-manager, Opus, fixed in passing).** *Ruling:* `stateChip` writes the instant through `stampLabel(…, bare)` against the page's `now`: today's stays `down since 12:40` as prototype-6 draws it, a monitor down since yesterday reads `down since yesterday 12:40` (was `down since 12:40`), an older one `down since 2026-10-12 12:40`. *Reasoning:* a fifth clock written in place, which dropped the day outright, so a monitor down since last night read as down since this afternoon. *Reversing:* low.

## #1998: a queued start-work step's button says *Check again* (implementer, Opus, 2026-10-24)

- **The wording.** *Fork:* prototype-6 and the TF conventions have no word for a button that re-reads a write without sending it, so the implementer picks one. *Ruling:* *Check again* on a queued step; a failed step keeps *Retry*. The footer's "A failed step can be retried, skipped or amended." stays as it is. *Reasoning:* the button calls `ready_retry`, whose rule 1 re-reads an open write's landing and dispatches nothing for it. The flow then runs on behind the answer, so the next steps go once this write has landed. Beside #1996's "it may have arrived -- check Jira, then send it again or discard it in the write queue", *Retry* reads as the second send #1973 says nothing should invite. *Check again* names the re-read and promises no second send. There is one gap. A step stored `queued` whose write was discarded or refused since falls through to rules 2 and 3 and can dispatch again. That is a Rust fix and changes the gate scope, so it is filed as #2015. The button stays because it is the only way a queued step moves on once its write lands. Recorded as a convention under *Writes and undo*. *Reversing:* one string in `TfStartWork.svelte`.
- **The class.** *Fork:* relabel this button alone, or every button whose label claims a send it does not make. *Ruling:* there is no other instance. *Reasoning:* the issue's searches, and a grep for `Retry`, `Re-run` and `Send again` labels in `app/src/lib`, find no other button that claims a send it does not make. The launcher's and board's *Retry* read the board or the sources again, the boot screen's restarts the database, `FirstRun.svelte`'s reruns a sync, and `MonitorDialog.svelte`'s resends a create that never queued (#1959). Each one repeats what failed. *Re-run* queues a build, and the write queue's *Send again* sends. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **Test seam.** *Ruling:* `TfJob.test.svelte.ts`, which mounts `TfStartWork` through the job page as the stepper's other tests do. The ticket names that seam. *Reasoning:* the loop runs unattended, so the seam is not confirmed with Björn first. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **Does *Check again* make #2015 worse?** (merge-manager, Opus) *Fork:* hold the label until #2015 lands, or merge it now. *Ruling:* merge it now and leave #2015 to its own ticket. *Reasoning:* the label is honest whenever the write is still open, whether it is waiting in the queue or unconfirmed, and that covers every queued step until someone discards or refuses its write in the write queue. The send in #2015's path is the same under either label, and rule 3's transition is safe to repeat, so the harm stays bounded until #2015 lands. *Retry* misread the common path, which is the one #1973 is about. The button's comment now names #2015, so the gap is visible beside the label. *Reversing:* one string.

## #2004: the `?fake-ipc` backend starts each test from its seed (implementer, Opus, 2026-10-24)

- **The fake is the exception to #1983's "plain `.ts` stays unscanned", under its own scan.** *Fork:* widen `test-resets.test.ts`' store scan to `shell/dev/fake/` with a `RESETS` key per value, or list one key in `UNSCANNED` and scan the fake on its own terms. *Ruling:* one key, `shell/dev/fake-seed.ts#restores`, in `UNSCANNED`. `dev/fake-seed.test.ts` scans `fake/` itself. *Reasoning:* the store scan's shapes miss most of the fake's state. That state is mostly `const` arrays and records a handler pushes to or splices, a shape #1983 left out because in the store files it is a constant table. The fake's scan flags any column-0 `let` that does not start at a number, plus any column-0 `const` that an indented line pushes to, sets, adds to, deletes from, splices or assigns an index of (an exported one in any module). Each flagged value must be named in that module's `keepSeed(...)` or assigned in its `onFakeReset(...)`. Load-time seeding (`CORPUS.push(...)` at column 0) does not count as a write. Other plain `.ts` files keep #1983's ruling: outside `dev/`, their column-0 sets are lookup tables. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **Where `resetFake()` lives and who calls it.** *Fork:* the ticket's two doors: call it from `installFakeTauri`, or add it to `RESETS`. *Ruling:* `RESETS` calls `resetFake()` in `shell/dev/fake-seed.ts`, which holds the restores each `fake/` module registers as it loads. *Reasoning:* `installFakeTauri` is the wrong door. Of the test files that load the fake, only `launcher-chain.test.svelte.ts` calls it: `fake-tauri.test.ts` and `fake-features.test.ts` call `demoHandlers()`, and `fake-corpus-query.test.ts` imports `fake/corpus.ts` directly. Also, `installIfRequested` runs every feature's `seed(params)` before it, so a reset there would wipe the `?fake-*` flags. A reset that imported `fake-tauri.ts` would load about 9,600 lines of fixture into all 188 test files. A file that never touches the fake loads only the 68-line registry, which is empty, and a module a test imports directly registers itself like the rest. *Reversing:* cheap.
- **The door goes behind `import.meta.env.DEV`, and the house rule's list grows.** *Ruling:* the reset's dynamic import sits behind the guard `house-rules.test.ts` asks of every importer of `shell/dev/`. `lib/shell/test-resets.ts` joins `App.svelte` and `capture.ts` on its list, with a comment. *Reasoning:* the rule keeps the fixture out of a bundle. No bundle loads `test-resets.ts`, but a quiet exemption for it would weaken the rule more than one more named door does. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **How a value goes back.** *Ruling:* in place, to a deep copy of what it held once the module had loaded. Arrays, maps, sets and plain objects are copied; functions are shared (the Jira fixture's `member` matchers, which `structuredClone` refuses). A module's `let`s are reassigned by its own `onFakeReset`, from one `seedOf({ … })` copy taken at load, so no starting value is written twice. The clone timers are cleared before the map empties. *Reasoning:* other modules hold the same arrays (`FIXTURE_ESTATE` is pushed by `estate-import.ts`, `FAKE_CONTEXTS` is read by `notes.ts`), so the array itself has to stay the same object. Handlers also edit elements in place (`asset.name = …`, `jira.source.hidden = …`), so a shallow refill would keep those edits. No module keeps an element of a kept array across a reset: every lookup is a `find` by id, and the one `indexOf` (`FIXTURE_EXTERNAL`) is on an object the seed does not hold. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **The class is 39 values, not the ticket's 29.** *Ruling:* all 39 are fixed here. The 10 the ticket did not list are `entity.ts#LINKS`, `estate.ts#FIXTURE_ESTATE`, `#FIXTURE_ROUTES` and `#ASSET_HISTORY`, `smart-lists.ts#FIXTURE_SAVED`, `sources.ts#FIXTURE_SOURCES`, `#FIXTURE_ADAPTERS` and `#INSTALLED`, and `ticket-views.ts#VIEWS` and `#JIRA`. The id counters keep counting (#1762). *Reasoning:* the scan finds them by the same rule, and each costs one name in a `keepSeed` call. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **The tests' own isolation is gone.** *Ruling:* `fake-tauri.test.ts` no longer calls `vi.resetModules()` in its two tests, and its comments no longer say a fresh `demoHandlers()` keeps the state. `fake-features.test.ts` no longer puts the shipped applications back by hand. *Reasoning:* each worked around this cause, and the comments became false. *Reversing:* trivial.
## #1989: small leftovers from checking the 2026-10-22 review's fixes (implementer, Opus, 2026-10-24)

- **Ruling #1626 amended, the window not bounded.** *Fork:* the ticket's two options, amend the
  reasoning with the per-configuration count or bound the window. *Ruling:* amended. The reasoning
  above said an ignored ceiling leaves "the few requests between the two queries" unprotected. For
  a source scoped to a configuration list the run reads `/projects` and `/buildTypes` and then asks
  once per configuration, so the window runs to the last configuration's `sinceBuild` query. That
  is `C + 2` requests or more for `C` configurations, about `C / 5` seconds at the default 5 req/s
  once the burst of 10 is spent, and 40 s for two hundred. The ceiling is ignored only when the
  opening pages show nothing as new as the watermark. On a server whose pages are unordered (#91)
  that is routine, not rare, so the exposure grows with `C`. `cursor::advance`'s docs now say so.
  *Reasoning:* bounding it changes what the opening probe asks and needs a seeded live run to
  confirm the locator, which is more than a leftover. The trade is still the one #1626 made,
  re-emission on every poll against a narrow loss: a build queued mid-run, still running at its
  configuration's query, while a later one finished before its own. Filed as #2016 with a
  direction (an incremental probe asking `sinceBuild` of the watermark). *Reversing:* low for the
  text; #2016 is the bound.
- **`inbox::Category` declared with `closed_vocabulary!`, not noted.** *Fork:* let the macro pass
  `ts_rs::TS` through, or note why the hand-rolled codec stays. *Ruling:* declared with the macro.
  *Reasoning:* the macro already passes enum attributes through, and `AssetStatus` derives
  `ts_rs::TS` that way, so the obstacle the ticket names was not there. The enum's own docs gave a
  different reason, no CHECK to pin. That covers only the migration test, not the one list `ALL`
  and `as_str` come from, and a category missing from the hand-written `ALL` was the drift the
  macro exists to rule out. The generated `InboxCategory` union is byte-for-byte unchanged. A
  decode failure now reads `unknown Category value`, through the shared `UnknownValue`.
  *Reversing:* low.
- **The flash-timer test counts timers.** *Fork:* witness the stray timer through what the reader
  sees, or through the timers left after the unmount. *Ruling:* the timers. *Reasoning:* the
  stray timer has no visible effect. After the second flash's own run returns early on
  `id === flashed`, the effect no longer reads `drawn`, so nothing reruns it when the first timer
  clears `flashed`. What is left is a timer that outlives the page, which is the PAGE-14 test's own
  measure. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **The double hold is fixed in `Registry::refuse`, not in `load_installed`.** *Ruling:* a refusal
  drops the loaded adapter of its kind. *Reasoning:* the restore's reinstall
  (`installed::reinstall_restored`) refuses through the same call over the same process registry,
  so the cause has two instances and one place. *Reversing:* low.
- **The reverse pin reads `apply_key_value`'s match arms from the source.** *Reasoning:* no probe
  can name a key nobody has listed yet. The scan takes the string literals that open an arm,
  between `match key {` and the `_ => return false` fallback, and compares them with
  `NEGATION_UNSUPPORTED_KEYS` as sets. *Reversing:* low.
- **`demo_load`'s `if let Ok(state) = sources::state(&app)` stays.** *Fork:* drop it with the
  assets arms as the same class. *Ruling:* kept. *Reasoning:* `tests/it/ipc.rs`'
  `demo_load_ends_with_a_terminal_sync_state_for_the_mock` reaches it with no sources state
  managed, and the arm writes nothing, it only skips the analyzer request. *Reversing:* low.
- **Test seams picked, not confirmed.** The TDD skill asks for the seams to be agreed first. Run
  unattended, they were picked: the Dependencies page mounted over stand-in ports, the house-rule
  matcher, the parser's own test module, bring-up over one registry (as LIFE-1's test does) plus
  `Registry::refuse`.
- **Can `Registry::refuse` drop an adapter a live source still uses?** (merge-manager, Opus)
  *Fork:* unload on refuse, or leave a loaded adapter in place until nothing holds it. *Ruling:*
  unload, as the PR does. *Reasoning:* a built source owns its adapter. `build` clones the
  `WasmAdapter` (an `Arc` of the compiled component) out from under the read lock, so a source
  that is running keeps the component it was built from after `refuse` takes the registry's copy
  away. What changes is the next `build` of that kind, which now fails with the refusal's reason.
  That is the ticket's ask, and Settings already calls the adapter refused at that point. On the
  restore path, the loaded adapter is the pre-restore one, and its artifact need not be the one
  the restored row pins, so building from it was wrong anyway. `replace` already empties the slot
  before its own check, so the two writers now agree. *Reversing:* low, one `retain`.
- **Amend #1626 rather than bound the window.** (merge-manager, Opus) *Ruling:* the amendment
  stands, and #2016 (backlog) is the bound. *Reasoning:* the ticket offers either option. The
  bound changes what TeamCity's opening probe asks, and only a seeded live run can confirm that
  the locator holds. That is a PR of its own, not a leftover. The amendment puts the real width
  where the next reader of `cursor::advance` will see it. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **The source-reading pin in `query.rs` is robust enough.** (merge-manager, Opus) *Ruling:*
  kept as written. *Reasoning:* rustfmt's reflow of a long pattern (`"a" | "b"` onto `| "c" =>`
  lines) parses the same way. A moved anchor (`fn apply_key_value(`, `match key {`, the
  `_ => return false,` fallback) panics by its `expect`. A literal standing alone on a body line
  counts as a key, which turns the test red, not green. The test reads green on a mutant only in
  two cases: an arm with a guard (`"x" if … =>`), and a nested `_ => return false,` above the
  fallback. Neither shape is in the function today, and either would go in front of a reviewer
  as a new arm. *Reversing:* low.
## #2013: every new cluster gets the builtin `C.UTF-8` locale at `initdb` (implementer, Opus, 2026-10-24)

Björn's triage on the issue decided the shape: the builtin provider's `C.UTF-8`, code-point order of titles accepted, existing clusters left alone, and no merge without a green Windows run. What follows is what came up beside it.

- **Confirmed under an empty environment, not from Finder.** *Ruling:* `initdb` and the app's bring-up were run under `env -i` and `LC_ALL=C` instead. With today's flags the bundled PostgreSQL 18.6 made a libc `C` cluster (`datlocprovider c`, `datcollate`/`datctype` `C`): `lower('ÜÄÖ')` stayed `ÜÄÖ`, `lower('İ')` stayed `İ`, `to_tsvector('english','Überweisung')` gave `'Überweisung'`, `show_trgm` dropped `Ü`, and `Zahlung` sorted before `apfel`. The new tests were red on main for the same reasons. Launching a packaged build from Finder is left to the milestone review. *Reasoning:* the dispatch says not to take the screen, and `initdb` reads only its environment, which `env -i` reproduces. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **Existing clusters: left alone.** *Fork:* the dispatch asks for detect-and-warn or a rebuild through backup and restore. *Ruling:* neither. Björn's triage says "Existing clusters are left alone. No detection, warning or rebuild." *Reasoning:* the ticket outranks the dispatch. The dispatch also names an ADR-0031 on search languages, but its PR (#2001) was closed unmerged, so ADR-0030 (`english` only) is the one in force. It changes nothing here. *Reversing:* a follow-up ticket, if Björn wants one.
- **The Windows C-library name is `en-US`.** *Ruling:* `--lc-collate=en-US --lc-ctype=en-US` on Windows, `C.UTF-8` elsewhere (`embedded::LIBC_LOCALE`). *Reasoning:* on `windows-latest`, `initdb` accepted it with `--encoding UTF8`, and the cluster read back `provider b, locale C.UTF-8, collate en-US, ctype en-US`. Both locale tests and #1843's two `knobas-search` tests passed there (runs 40098606066, on the first commit, and 40100283379, on the PR's final code `f1ed7670` with the workflow added back on a throwaway branch). Windows has no `C.UTF-8` C-library locale. *Reversing:* one string per category.
- **`lc_messages`, `lc_monetary`, `lc_numeric` and `lc_time` still come from the environment.** *Ruling:* not pinned. *Reasoning:* they are server settings, not fixed when a database is created, and the ticket names only collation and ctype. Nothing in knobas reads their effects: no code matches server message text, and the one `to_char` (`knobas-core/src/inbox.rs`) uses no `TM` pattern. The bundled macOS build also has no NLS. *Reversing:* `--locale=…` in place of the two flags.
- **`İ` under the builtin provider.** *Ruling:* no change needed. *Reasoning:* `lower('İ')` is `i` (one character) under builtin `C.UTF-8`, the same as under libc `en_US.UTF-8` on macOS. #1843's tests (`a_value_…`/`a_word_with_a_dotted_capital_i_matches_under_the_servers_fold`, `a_pattern_with_a_dotted_capital_i_matches_under_the_servers_fold`, `a_review_asked_of_a_dotted_capital_i_user_is_on_the_card_and_in_has`) pass unchanged on the new clusters, and so does every #1993 test in the full `just test` run. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **The full-text probe is `english`.** *Ruling:* the test checks `to_tsvector('english', 'Überweisung')`. `german` was probed by hand and gives `'uberweis'`. *Reasoning:* ADR-0030 makes `english` the only configuration the mirror indexes under. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **No test pinned a libc order.** *Ruling:* none updated. *Reasoning:* `just test` on the new flags passed 4,021 tests with 0 failures in 57 binaries, every one of them on a freshly made builtin `C.UTF-8` test server. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **Test seams.** *Ruling:* `EmbeddedDb::start`, the bring-up the app runs, inside a child re-run of the test binary with `LC_ALL`, `LANG`, `LC_CTYPE`, `LC_COLLATE` and `LC_MESSAGES` set to `C`. *Reasoning:* a test cannot change its own process's environment safely while others run beside it, and the child pattern is already in `tests/embedded.rs`. The loop runs unattended, so the seams were picked rather than confirmed. *Reversing:* n/a.

- **`LIBC_LOCALE` and `en-US` on Windows.** *Ruling:* kept. *Reasoning:* Windows has no C-library `C.UTF-8`, and the ticket names `en-US` as the candidate. Run 40100283379 ran on `e8c67de3`, whose `crates/` tree is the PR head's, and read back `provider b, locale C.UTF-8, collate en-US, ctype en-US` with both locale tests and #1843's two `knobas-search` tests passing. ## #2015: *Check again* on a queued start-work step whose write closed since settles it failed (implementer, Opus, 2026-10-24)

- **Which outcome the settle may leave.** *Fork:* the closed-write settle could leave any outcome a retry may leave (`RETRIES`), or only `queued`. *Ruling:* only `queued`. *Reasoning:* the step is settled failed because it read `queued` and its button promised a re-read. If another action moved it on between that read and the write, settling it failed would overwrite that action, so the settle refuses and the stepper re-reads, as any stale retry does (#1707). *Reversing:* one constant in `ready_retry`.
- **A pending step with a closed write.** *Fork:* the ticket names `queued` (settle) and `failed` (today's path). A `pending` step carrying a write id, which is a failed step a retry reset, has no button of its own. *Ruling:* it keeps today's path. *Reasoning:* only a queued step's button reads *Check again*. A pending step is what the run takes next, so it goes through rules 2 and 3 as before. *Reversing:* one condition.
- **Frontend.** *Fork:* add a refresh to `TfStartWork` after the settle, or rely on the retry's answer. *Ruling:* no frontend change beyond the button's comment. *Reasoning:* `start_work_retry` answers the flow after `ready_retry` has settled, and `act` draws that answer, so the row redraws as *failed* with *Retry* and the discard's sentence. `TfJob.test.svelte.ts` pins it. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **Test seam.** *Ruling:* `tests/it/start_work.rs` against the `Steps` fake, as the ticket names, and `TfJob.test.svelte.ts` for the redraw. The loop runs unattended, so the seams are not confirmed with Björn first. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **The `REREADS` guard, unwitnessed** (merge-manager, Opus) *Fork:* merge with the guard pinned only for admitting `queued`, or witness the direction the implementer left open. *Ruling:* witness it. *Reasoning:* the fake's landing read can run a second stepper's *Check again* and *Retry* between the first re-read's `step_of` and its settle, which leaves the step `pending` the way a real second window would. `checking_again_on_a_step_another_stepper_moved_on_is_refused_and_sends_nothing` asserts the conflict, the step left `pending`, and no send; widening the guard to `RETRIES` fails it. The guard is upheld: a `pending` step at that point is the other retry's, and settling it failed would undo it. *Reversing:* drop one test.
- **A pending step with a closed write keeps today's path** (merge-manager, Opus) *Fork:* uphold the implementer's ruling, or send a `pending` step with a closed write through the re-read too. *Ruling:* upheld. *Reasoning:* a step is `pending` with a write id only after a retry reset a failed step, and the stepper draws no button on a pending step, so nothing that promised a re-read reaches it. It is the run's next step, and rules 2 and 3 are what the run does with it: read the mirror, then send. Settling it failed would stop a retry the user just asked for. *Reversing:* one condition.
## #2008: the mirror argument tests read the call's keys (implementer, Opus, 2026-10-24)

- **A key needs a `:`, `,` or `}` after it too.** *Fork:* the ticket defines a key by the character before it (`{` or `,`). *Ruling:* `mirror::keys` also requires the next non-space character to be `:`, `,` or `}`, and reads only after the call's `>(`. *Reasoning:* the ticket's rule alone counts `b` in a value `f(a, b)` and a generic's `B` in `<A, B>` as keys, so a test could pass on a name that is not sent. The stricter rule still covers both the shorthand and `key: value`. *Reversing:* drop one `matches!`.
- **`mini_board`'s argument checks moved too.** *Ruling:* the two `entity/mod.rs` tests read `keys(invocation(MIRROR, "mini_board"))` and no longer split the call text by hand. *Reasoning:* the dispatch asks for every argument check to use the reader. The ticket rules `contains("savedView: ")` out as an instance, but it fails a correct shorthand `{ savedView }`, and `!contains("sources")` would match a value named `sources`. *Reversing:* trivial.
- **Test seams.** *Ruling:* `mirror::keys` on literal call texts, plus the three barrel tests on the real `.ts` files. *Reasoning:* the loop runs unattended, so I picked the seams instead of getting them confirmed. *Reversing:* n/a.
## #2016: the TeamCity opening probe asks from the watermark on (implementer, Opus, 2026-10-24)

- **Measured before relying on the direction.** *Fork:* build on the ticket's suggested locator, or measure it first. *Ruling:* measured, as the ticket asks. *Reasoning:* the findings follow, and the next ruling rests on them. On the seeded TeamCity 2026.1.3 (build 222742), 2026-10-24, read-only apart from one build queued and deleted again: `sinceBuild:(id:N),defaultFilter:false` with no `state:` answered exactly the builds above `N` across every configuration, a running build included, and `count: 0` above the newest. `count:2` over three matches reported a `nextHref`. An `N` that names no build was read as a number every time, never a 404: a gap in the ids, one past the top, one below the oldest, and the build deleted a minute earlier. The queued state passed before the first poll, so the probe was seen only with a running build. The ceiling does not rest on queued builds being on that page, because the in-flight poll lists them. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **`sinceBuild:(id:W-1)`, not `sinceBuild:(id:W)`.** *Fork:* the ticket's direction asks for the watermark itself. *Ruling:* one below it, so the watermark's own build is on the page. A watermark of 1 or less asks no `sinceBuild` at all, which is the same page. *Reasoning:* `sinceBuild` is exclusive. With `W`, an idle poll's page is empty, so `refuse_a_replaced_server` sees nothing reach the watermark and asks `/app/rest/builds/id:W` on every idle poll, one request more per source per poll. `a_run_whose_pages_reach_the_watermark_asks_nothing_by_id` rules that out. An empty page also proves nothing, because the server reads a missing `W` as a number. With `W` the empty page's ceiling is also `None`, which clamps nothing: the mutant that asks from `W` fails the new test. The ticket's "the watermark itself is a valid ceiling" would then need a second rule. From `W-1` the page holds `W` whenever the build is there, so the refusal's trigger is the one it was and the ceiling is never below the watermark. *Reversing:* low, one expression.
- **`cursor::advance` applies a ceiling below the watermark again.** *Fork:* keep #1626's "ignored" arm, which no longer fires, or remove it. *Ruling:* removed, and the floor holds the watermark where it stands. This reverses #1626's arm, not its trade: the trade was re-emission on every poll against a narrow loss, and the probe now avoids both. *Reasoning:* the arm fires only when the opening pages show nothing as new as the watermark. From the watermark on, that happens only when the build is gone, which `refuse_a_replaced_server` refuses, or on a server whose `sinceBuild` misses a build it holds. No measured server does that. On such a server a re-fetch on every poll can be seen, while a lost build cannot. *Reversing:* low, one `filter`.
- **The by-id check stays, and its "found" branch has no unit test.** *Ruling:* kept. `a_watermark_the_pages_did_not_show_is_confirmed_by_id_and_the_run_proceeds` becomes `a_watermark_behind_an_unordered_page_is_witnessed_by_the_probe`. It shows the same hundred-row page no longer hides the watermark, and that nothing is asked by id. *Reasoning:* the refusal's message cites the server's 404, so it needs the fetch. A stand-in that answers `sinceBuild` correctly cannot reach "found", and one that answers it wrongly would be a claim about TeamCity that the measurement above contradicts. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **Re-emission is bounded at one poll.** *Ruling:* accepted. A run whose emitted builds were all queued after it opened leaves the watermark where it was, and the next run's probe sees them and moves it on. The new sync test runs both polls. `a_ceiling_below_the_watermark_does_not_hold_it_under_builds_just_emitted` (#1626) still passes unchanged: from the watermark on, its page holds the twelve builds. Its name described a ceiling the probe no longer produces, so it is renamed `an_unordered_page_does_not_hold_the_watermark_under_builds_just_emitted`. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **Live witness.** *Ruling:* `the_opening_probe_from_the_watermark_holds_its_build_and_every_newer_one` joins the seeded suite. It is read-only and pins the three answers the `Rest` stand-in assumes. The existing watermark test runs the probe on a real idle poll, on a real new build and on the deleted build's 404 refusal. *Reversing:* drop one test.
- **Test seams.** *Ruling:* `sync::execute` over `MidRun`, which now takes more than two instants (`then`) and can serve fixture order, plus `cursor::advance` and the seeded live suite. The loop runs unattended, so I picked the seams and did not get them confirmed. *Reversing:* n/a.

### #2016 review rulings (merge-manager, Opus, 2026-10-24)

- **Authority for the reversal.** *Fork:* spec #1618's Solution says "The cursor advance ignores a ceiling below the previous watermark", and #1626 is an unattended ruling built on it; ticket #2016 asks that the ceiling never be ignored. *Ruling:* within an agent's authority. The ticket loop orders ticket body over parent spec, #2016 is the more specific source, and since 2026-10-22 an Opus implementer or merge-manager rules a frozen-contract change (`docs/agents/working-model.md`). The §4.2 amendment now names the spec sentence it supersedes, and spec #1618 carries a comment saying so. *Reasoning:* the spec sentence described the remedy #1626 chose for the unfiltered probe; with the probe from the watermark the case it guarded no longer arises on a correct server. *Reversing:* prose, plus #2016's one `filter`.
- **The "found" branch gets a unit test after all.** *Fork:* the implementer ruled that no stand-in reaches it without a false claim about TeamCity. *Ruling:* a `FakeRest` flag, `probe_misses_since_build`, serves the probe unfiltered; `a_probe_that_misses_the_watermark_is_confirmed_by_id_and_holds_it_where_it_stands` runs the branch end to end. *Reasoning:* the stand-in claims nothing about TeamCity; it is the server the ruling above names as the only one where the branch and the floor matter, and without it a mutant that refuses on "found" survived every test. *Reversing:* drop one test and one flag.
- **A busy, unordered server advances in steps, not stalls.** *Fork:* the probe page is one page of 100 from the watermark on, so its maximum can sit below the true top. *Ruling:* accepted, no change. *Reasoning:* the page holds 100 distinct ids at or above the watermark, so the ceiling is at least `W + 99` when it is full and the true top at run start when it is not; the watermark never stalls, and the shortfall is the re-fetch the ceiling already accepts. Against the old unfiltered page in the same order, the filtered page's maximum is never lower whenever the old one reached the watermark. *Reversing:* n/a.
## #2003: Jira's board listing is read twice (implementer, Opus, 2026-10-24)

- **List twice, not the anchored walk.** *Fork:* the ticket's two shapes, picked by the measured order. *Ruling:* list twice, as Gitea does. *Reasoning:* on the seeded Jira 10.3, `GET /rest/agile/1.0/board` lists boards by name, ignoring case: boards made `m`, `A`, `z` (ids rising that way) come back `A`, `m`, `z`, `orderBy=id`, `orderBy=-id` and `orderBy=-name` change nothing, and `A` renamed `zz` (through `PUT /rest/greenhopper/1.0/rapidviewconfig/name`) moves to the end. A rename moves a row, so the anchoring in `walk.rs` has no order to stand on. Pinned by `live_jira_seeded::the_board_listing_is_in_name_order_and_a_rename_moves_a_row` (the name order, `orderBy=id` and the rename; the other two `orderBy` values were probed by hand in the same measurement). *Reversing:* `views::listing`, one function.
- **Every board read lists twice, not only a full sync.** *Fork:* Gitea lists twice on a full sync alone. *Ruling:* every run that reads the boards. *Reasoning:* `sync.rs` sends `views::gone` for each view the previous cursor held and this read did not, on incremental runs too, so every board read licenses a tombstone. The cost is one more listing request per project (or one for every board) per board read, which an idle source makes at most hourly (#1700). *Reversing:* a flag to `listing`.
- **Twice, not until two listings agree.** *Ruling:* two passes, as #2006's merge review kept for Gitea. *Reasoning:* a miss needs a second change landing on the same row in the second pass, and lasts until the next board read. *Reversing:* the loop bound.
- **The newer record wins a board met in both passes.** *Ruling:* the second pass's boards go first, so `boards`' stable sort and `dedup_by_key` keep them. *Reasoning:* a board renamed between the passes is delivered under its new name at once instead of at the next read. `a_board_renamed_between_the_two_listings_arrives_under_its_new_name` covers it. *Reversing:* swap two lines.
- **"None reported gone" read as "no other board".** *Fork:* the ticket's probe says a deleted board "leaves every other board read and none reported gone". *Ruling:* the probe asserts the run delivers exactly the deleted board, as gone. *Reasoning:* that board is gone from Jira, and delivering it as gone is the behaviour `a_board_deleted_in_jira_is_delivered_as_gone_at_the_next_sync` pins; on main the run also delivered `board-151`, the board shifted past the offset, as gone. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **A rename probe beside the deletion probe.** *Ruling:* added. *Reasoning:* the measured order makes a rename the second way to hide a board (one renamed from an unread page into a read one). *Reversing:* drop one test.
- **The fake lists in Jira's order.** *Ruling:* `views::tests::Agile` sorts its listing by name, ignoring case, and can switch to a second board list once the first page is answered. *Reasoning:* the fake is a claim about Jira, checked once against the real one by the live pin. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **One guard for both live probes.** *Ruling:* the refused-query probe's guard became `Probes`, with the board-order probe as its second constructor, rather than a copy of it. *Reasoning:* both own a list of `Probed` and take it back through `take_back`; only the cleanup's wording differed. *Reversing:* n/a.
- **Test seam.** *Ruling:* `SyncRun::run` over the `Agile` fake, PAY alone (the fake answers every board for each project, so a second project's listing would hide the bug). The loop runs unattended, so the seam was picked rather than confirmed. *Reversing:* n/a.
